speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion, under Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. As imports from low-wage countries are taking away a steadily increasing share of the Canadian market from Canadian products, thus causing Canadian workers to be laid off in ever-increasing numbers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling):

That this House direct the Minister of Finance to introduce import quotas, to be applied against imports from low-wage countries in order to retain the same high proportion of the Canadian market for Canadian producers as the United States and European Common Market do to protect their domestic producers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. As the minister knows, or should know, the Indian and Inuit people of this country have health problems of a magnitude far greater than the general population of Canada.
How can the minister justify unilateral action which will affect adversely the health of Indians and Inuit in Canada and the delivery of health services to these people without consulting the Indian community? By way of example, I mention the 30 maritime Indian chiefs who are in Ottawa at the present time and with whom the minister has refused to meet despite repeated representations by myself and, in particular, by my Conservative colleagues from the Atlantic provinces.

speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member raises a question about the identification or the granting of an opportunity during question period for persons to participate in the question period. Of course, that is never a question of privilege; it is a matter which lies within the sole discretion of the Chair. That is the way it must remain. It is not a question of privilege and cannot be under any circumstances.

The second matter raised by the hon. member has to do solely with procedure within the standing committee, which is not within my jurisdiction to deal with in any manner as long as the matter is before the committee. If any hon. member at any time has any grievance to raise about his rights being affected adversely in any way by any decisions or procedures of the committee, they must be resolved in that committee. The committees have the power to set their own rules in any way they wish. If there is a grievance, it may come before this House at the time the committee reports to the House; or if the matter is raised in the standing committee and in itself as a grievance becomes part of a report when it is reported to the House, then the House can take it into account. But as long as the proceedings remain in the committee, the decisions to govern its own procedures remain the business of the committee and not the business of the Chair.

The House resumed from Wednesday, December 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Trudeau:
That the following address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada:
To His Excellency the Right Honourable Jules Leger, Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of Canada.
May it please Your Excellency:
The House of Commons, having considered the proposed text of the order in council laid upon the table of the House on December 4, 1978, in relation to the establishment of a Ministry of State for Economic Development, prays that the making of the said order in council be approved.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem we are dealing with today in setting up a new ministry of state to provide authority for one minister to speak on behalf of the co-ordinated policies of the government is not a new problem to any government in the world. I should think it is safe to say that since the war in every country of the
1973-	1974
1974-	1975

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
world that has some form of representative government, and that includes communist states, there has been a battle for power between those who have elected positions of power, such as the communist power in Russia or in China, and the elected members of parliament and the cabinet as in countries of the west.
I had the privilege of discussing this matter with the senior members of the People's Republic of China in 1964. It is not a new problem there. They were worried in their new government how to control the tremendous bureaucracy which had to be developed to do all the things the government has had to do involving the business of the country.
Likewise I have had discussions with senior members of the Russian hierarchy. As I remember those conversations, this resulted in the cultural revolution in China in 1966-67 where high school students and university students were freed from school to go out and attack their teachers and civil servants, with the hope that by yelling at them they might get across the message that they were supposed to be carrying out the policies of the people and not policies to perpetuate themselves.
This problem relating to the control of bureaucracy has been in existence here in Canada as well. Those of us who were here from 1962 to 1968 will remember the technique used by the Pearson administration. That administration saw this problem as one of political science. When there was a problem that could not be met, that administration created a new department. This resulted, I think it is fair to state, in a weakening of some of the in line or regular departments, such as the Department of Agriculture, with various functions belonging to the regular departments being put into these separate portfolios.
Nothing new came from this practice except a continual flow of ministers. I suppose if you looked at the length of time served by ministers of various portfolios under both the Pearson and the present administration, you would find that never before in the history of Canada were ministers able to serve for such a short period of time.
I point that out for a reason. It was very evident in the days of the Pearson administration that there had to be some control by elected representatives over those who were fully paid representatives, civil servants if you like, in this country. The reason for this can be found in previous history. It actually goes back to the 1930s following which there was a reform of the civil service. The Bennett administration brought in a top notch man with instructions to build the best civil service possible in Canada. Mr. Clark was recruited to build that civil service. There is a statue here in Ottawa, quite properly, as a result of that service. He brought together in the 1930s and into the war period some of the best minds from universities and businesses across the land, which enabled Canada to go through the war without even going into high gear. We went through the war in a cruising posture because of the efficiency of the direction of the civil servants here in Ottawa. It was a high level mark in the running of a government by paid employees of the Crown.

As time went on and ministers became accustomed to accepting directions and ideas from the civil service, we have this management concept of government taking hold. The ministers in the latter period of the Mackenzie King government became accustomed to taking orders which came up from their departments, presenting them to cabinet and having Mr. Howe look at them and nod his acceptance. In the St. Laurent period the same thing occurred even more smoothly. He was quite content to hand the details of any policy over to the civil servants who would propose their ideas to their ministers, and if Mr. Howe nodded his head then it went through.
This was the situation when a new government was elected in 1957. Clearly this new government had different policy points of view which were tied around the word "development". Historically, this was the traditional position of the Conservative party, and we had this program of development and all its concomitant policies ready to go. However, these policies had not originated in the traditional civil service milieu of officials who had been accustomed to administering the country purely as a managerial function.
This clash between the elected representatives and the appointed representatives of the people came to a head in what is now known as the Coyne episode. When the budget was read in 1959, cabinet ministers were surprised to find that the policies enunciated in it were the opposite to what the cabinet wanted to do. There was a discussion with the people who devised this policy which went on through the winter of 1959 into the summer of 1960. As a result of those discussions, Mr. Coyne refused to accept the government's expansionary policies, the government would not accept his restrictive policies, and we had to announce our intention in parliament to have him dismissed. This was probably the first clash in the history of the western world between the elected representatives and the senior mandarins of the civil service regarding their respective ideals.
This decision on the part of the Diefenbaker administration probably cost them the reins of government because a feeling went through the establishment of the civil service, business, university and all the opinion leaders across this country which was expressed in this way: "How can this country be run by a group of prairie cowboys?" Actually we were right. Our policy at that time set this country moving in an upward direction economically that lasted from 1961 to 1968, the longest period of sustained wealth foundation growth in the history of our country.
Because of that clash and because of the fact that the cause of the civil service was defeated, it was only good sense on the part of the Pearson administration to take a look at this situation to see how they could get control and have some say over the civil service, which had welcomed Mr. Pearson back into the fold as one of the same flock of sheep that had been there for a long time. That was the beginning of this war which has gone on continuously.
December 14, 1978

As I have said, this war is not only going on in Canada. Prime Minister Wilson of Great Britain, during his administration, decided to put four or five top men in charge of groups of portfolios. Hon. members can read all about that disaster in his book, which he wrote after he lost the prime ministership and went into retirement.
Approximately six or seven years ago, in 1971 the Ontario government set up four co-ordinating ministers-as a matter of fact, one of them sits in this House today-who were to co-ordinate the work of several ministries. One needs only to speak to them to learn the results of that attempt to control departments and thereby control civil servants.
In the year 1974-the United States government, faced with the energy crisis, appointed an economic and energy czar in the name of William Simon. He is no longer in that position but he has written a book called "It is Time to Tell the Truth". Every parliamentarian in the world should read that book, which outlines how a brilliant man set up as a czar was beaten by the forces that were in place. All the techniques of delay were used. There were pressure groups, and there was complete subjugation of the leading publishers and the media of the country. They had to fit in with the establishment or they were not in.
This is something I have already mentioned, and it brings me to the present administration. The best way to understand the situation is to let your mind go back ten years when the new emperor took power. The first thing that he did was to realize that the civil service had to be controlled, and as a result the Prime Minister's office was set up. It was a deliberately planned effort to give himself and the people around him enough knowledge and power that they could direct, instead of taking direction from the bottom, from the same tired, old group of people who had made their last serious effort in 1946 to be constructive and innovative. That was the way the government worked from 1968 to 1972 when it had a majority. The Prime Minister's office put up a gallant fight to match the controls of the Privy Council, which has now grown very big and powerful and put up a fight against the tremendous knowledge and strength of the various departments in the civil service.
In 1972 there was a minority government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) must have blamed his failure to get a majority on the fact that the people believed that the Privy Council Office or his Prime Minister's office was not doing a good job of running the country. In effect, he scuttled for a period of time his Prime Minister's office and began to draw more heavily on the civil service mandarins, particularly those in the Privy Council office.
If one looks at the events over those years and then looks at the events of the last four years when the majority was restored to the government, one gets a good picture why this order in council is before parliament today. This government has been guided for ten years by a two-fold philosophy. Part of it is that by political science techniques, by putting boxes on a diagram and arrows in those boxes, this will solve the problem.
Economic Development
The Prime Minister is on public record as having declared that as his policy.
The Prime Minister thinks that all we need to do to run this government is to appoint knowledgeable people to run it and then he can sit back and take his holidays skin diving or whatever. This is the managerial concept gone mad, the concept of all control going to the Prime Minister through his Privy Council office, to the Prime Minister's office and the civil service, and making an occasional report to cabinet.
I have rushed through this history of the last 16 years. I will simply say that the last episode of August 1 when the Prime Minister came back from Bonn and Morocco and announced a $2 billion restraint program, which ministers will get the civil service to bring in, indicates that the Prime Minister's battle, will simply be continued in a continuing war with the civil service.
If we visualize this as a war for power, we begin to see the picture a little more clearly. Ministers were called back from their holidays and told that the government wanted a $2 billion restraint program rammed through. The ministers did not know what to do. They cannot do anything because they know nothing to start with. When they were asked to do this, they called on their deputy ministers and told them that the Prime Minister wanted them to save a certain number of dollars. The civil service showed who was boss. They picked where the cuts would take place. They decided that the forestry service in Petawawa should go. That does not affect any of their friends in Ottawa. They decided that fisheries research should go and that ARDA should go. All these things were put in place by parliament to help the country make more money and fight inflation. They were wiped out partly as a policy of the civil service to show that it could take these instructions and do whatever it liked and, to use street language, screw the government in the process.
The government is taking an awful beating in terms of public opinion over the so-called restraint program. On some occasions it has even tried to back away from it. The civil service has won the war, although at times they seem to be losing it. I will return to this point and give some details at the end of my remarks.
A word or two should be said about the position of the Progressive Conservative party. I have related the Coyne episode on many occasions because it is crucial to an understanding of what we were trying to do. In our innocence we were trying to demonstrate that we, as elected representatives of the people, having decided on a fundamental policy of expansion, wanted the country to expand and did not intend to let any senior official of the civil service or any department or agency stand in our way. What we did was right and proper but we paid a heavy price for it in the next election in the cities where propaganda works most effectively.
It has to be made clear, as the key point of my remarks, that the only time an elected government ever stood up against the civil service was in that episode in 1959. That is why I stand

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
here today in support of our leader, the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark), whom I expect very shortly to take over the job of prime minister of this country.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I look back over the experiences of the last 30-odd years from the high point of the civil service in 1946 to where it is now, running like a bunch of sheep from one corral to another-we all know the sheep are going to end up in the same place before they are clipped. Then 1 look at this young man who leads the official opposition today. I speak from the experience of having known and seen in action Mackenzie King, St. Laurent, Pearson and the present Prime Minister. I have watched and worked with men like John Bracken, George Drew, John Diefenbaber, Robert Stanfield and our present leader, and I do not think I misstate the case at all when I say unequivocally that, in my judgment, our present leader is the best qualified and best prepared person out of these nine to settle this war between the elected representatives and the civil service. I knew his interests when he worked for various ministers in government as well as in the opposition. I know something of his thinking as to making it possible for the will of the people to be restored in Canada through their elected representatives.
This is not the type of thing that is talked about on every street corner; it is a battle, a war that is going on across the world. In our part of the war, in Canada, I think we have a leader in the Conservative party who has a better chance of understanding how to utilize the tremendous merit and strength of our civil service and move it into the innovative and creative thinking of the Conservative party, thus producing a winning team.
We must be aware of power groups, however, Over the last 30 or 40 years in Canada, business has had tremendous power and since the war labour has developed tremendous power. We have a new rival for power-the media in radio and television, and even the newspaper have a little left. Since 1956, these people no longer report the news. They are an editorial power group who feel their views on what should be done are closer to the truth than the views of the elected representatives in the government or the opposition. They must be accepted as a rival for power. They have long since lost the innocence of reporting the news in a factual manner and, in effect, have moved into the job of the opposition. Their excuse is that we are not strong enough to get our opposition across so they will decide what has to be done.
I sat in this House during this last session and witnessed one or two very good debates. Just two weeks ago there was a debate on the motion of the Social Credit party and every person who spoke in that debate actually spoke on the subject of the motion. That is very unusual. But what was usual about that debate was the fact there was no news of it. A debate on a subject of very great importance apparently is not news.
In the present circumstances the only news that is reported is on the techniques of the government. That is all they study-public relations. Members on that side use every trick

of the trade to get their names in the newspapers, on television and on radio. They crawl around here like hyperactive ants trying to get their faces on television or their voices on radio. A minister is not selected on the basis of what he or she knows or can do, but on the basis of ability to communicate. We end up with a group of communicators running the country. Their skill is what I have just described, namely, getting it out. It does not make any difference whether it says anything sensible-just get it out. Naturally, ambitious young members of parliament think this is the way things are done, but to win the battle I am talking about it is necessary to have someone or a group in any party know something about something.
I suggest that the leader of this party knows that he must have people around him who know something about something and are prepared to put their experience into practice. He knows that he must have around him someone who knows something about resources, because this is a resource country. He also knows that this person must appreciate that we live in an interdependent world. We must know the extent of world resources, the demand for those resources and the supplies available. Above that there must be an industrial strategy based on those resources. Such an industrial strategy must have its priorities and its related policies in finance, trade, manpower and development, and there must be co-ordination of all these factors.
This is the type of thing that I think the young leader of the Conservative party is aware of. He knows that he must have people around him in all fields, not just resources, who know something about their subject. That is the only way to cope with the tremendous efficiency and know-how of the civil service. Everything we want to do must draw on those assets- the know-how, ability and knowledge of the civil service. We must put them to work formulating policy on those subjects in line with the philosophy of the government of the day.
The leader of our party knows the history of the civil service in Ottawa. He has been around here for 20 years and he knows that the civil service has failed to grow in ideas since 1946. That is where the weakness is. He knows that to climb in the civil service one has to belong to a pyramid and keep one's nose at the right angle to make progress. This conformity principle that is so strongly entrenched in the civil service bars from that upward movement many of the ideas and know-how that are there in the civil service. Who knows about this situation better than the present leader of the Conservative party? I know of no other person.
I would like to mention next the public relations propensity of the present government. Ever since the days of Mr. Pearson the governing party has put the emphasis on public relations. There was a problem in 1963 so they brought in a whole team of fellows as evidence that they had strong men around Mr. Pearson who could run this country. They had a picture of a bus which shows all these bright young fellows getting off the bus with briefcases and suitcases with all their plans ready. When the government changed in 1963 they walked back and
December 14, 1978

forth from the East Block to this block, carrying some document or reading a book-not the red book of Mao, but the same thing, and a lot bigger. They were going to give us 60 days of decison. Actually it was an image for the public.
The first decision came in the budget on the fifty-seventh day, and one of the better qualified ministers of that government came a cropper because he forgot one little detail. And that detail? If you bring in an outsider who knows something about what you want to do and have him do it for you, you get rid of him a few days before the budget is announced or you will be under the suggestion of a leak. What we are witnessing here today is the present version of the same technique of the bus with all these young fellows getting off it and pretending they are busy and that they will be able to solve everything in 60 days. All they have is an idea in this order in council. It is that if we could only get the ministers who deal with economic matters to sit down together under one minister who could co-ordinate their efforts and put their views before the cabinet, then we would solve our economic problems.
Let us take a look at this image they are now trying to create. Remember that nothing succeeds so poorly as the blind trying to lead the blind. But this is what we are witnessing. They have even left out the portfolios of agriculture, forestry and fisheries. It never crossed the minds of the political scientists who drafted the order in council that a great part of the wealth of this nation over the next few decades will be coming from the production of food, fibre and energy. Nearly half of the energy for the future needs of Canada will be drawn by farmers. Yet the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is left out. I am not suggesting the Minister of Agriculture could make any contribution, but there may be some people in his department who know what is possible, and biomass is more than just a swear word, it is a very valuable product. I would like to have seen some realization of this by those who drafted the order in council. In image-making one always slips up.
As I look at this matter, I also look at things which have happened before, and I am not alone in my observations. I refer, for example, to the federal-provincial ministry that was set up in 1977. Most members can remember back that far. I have a story from a local paper, the Journal, dated September 27, 1977. The article is written by a man who served as one of the inner group in government; he is now a pundit. The headline reads "Bureaucrats Wins Latest Round Against Top Federal Ministers." What else have I been talking about for the last 20 minutes? Let me read some selections from this article. The first one states:
I am informed ... that the federal-provincial relations office will continue to report directly to the Prime Minister, but will work closely,... very closely, with the Minister of Federal-Provincial Relations.
That is gobbledy-gook. It means they have made a new man the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Reid) but that he and the department are to always report to the Prime Minister. Here is a situation where a federal cabinet minister is appointed who has no civil servants at all. Mr. Economic Development
Gwyn, the author of the article, goes on to describe the political in-fighting. He says:
The interest in the battle of the Dotted Line is that it has matched Ottawa's best political in-fighter against the town's best bureaucratic in-fighter. The significance in the affair is that the bureaucrat won. If you still cling to to that quaint theory that cabinet ministers run the mandarins, now is the time to chuck it.
Let us take another example, that of the committee system.
I have an article from the Citizen dated January 26, 1978. 1 have clippings here over the last 15 years, but I am not going to go into all of them. This article is about a top mandarin. At the particular time he was president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. He gave a speech to the Institute of Public Administration of Canada. His speech was very similar to the remarks made by the deputy minister of finance. This was the statement, and I quote:
-innovation and creativity are being frustrated by committee style policy-making.
This was the belief of Simon Reisman and A1 Johnson, two top mandarins, one in the field of finance and the other in the field of broadcasting, who were complaining about the committee system. Taking the speech in detail, 1 will quote one paragraph:
-the representative committee approach almost inevitably creates a bargaining situation ... Sometimes this means the acceptance of constraints before the advantages of new policy directions can be measured against possible changes in constraints; sometimes it means a succession of compromises which lead to the lowest common policy denominator. Or both.
Here is an example of civil servants complaining about this system and about being so frustrated. One more layer is put in here and another one put in there to make sure there is enough bargaining for all groups, but nothing will be done. That is a translation of that quote, which is a quotation from a speech delivered to the Institute of Public Administration of Canada around January 26, 1978.
I could go on and on. I have talked a little bit about Pearson's new departments every month. I could talk about the Trudeau technique of shifting portfolios. Politically it is simply a device called the "moving target principle of responsibility". If you have ten ministers running across the stage over a ten-year period, it is hard to get a lead on them and catch them. One is out of the damned picture before you can get a lead on the next.
These poor ministers do not get a chance to learn their portfolios. You cannot blame the civil servants for saying they come and they go but we stay on forever. That is how you lose control over the people you are supposed to be directing. That is what the Leader of the Opposition meant yesterday when he called it the downgrading of cabinet. This cabinet has changed so fast that all you can think of is a bunch of assorted Grits in a pot.

speechtext: Like shaking a box of Rice Krispies.

I think I have made my point about this legislation. We are being asked to conclude that by putting in a czar we will end all this confusion, that by doing that their struggle for power will be

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
won. I am simply saying, "Oh, no, you are not." It is simply a part of the struggle and everyone knows it. When it is all over, the headlines will come out "Civil servants still in control".
With regard to the suggestion of a super minister, there is only one thing in the whole statement that intrigues me. I quote from page 2 of the order in council, at the bottom of the page:
His Excellency in Council is further pleased to direct-
(b) He shall advise the Treasury Board on the allocation of financial,
personnel and other resources to federal programs that provide direct support
to the development of economic enterprise in Canada;
The word "shall" sounds impressive. It means you must ask advice. However, the question has to be asked, do you have to take that advice? Does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) really think he is going to sit at the head of his department and let this group walk all over the top of the department? The Department of Finance will show who is boss. They have been running the show here for 20 years. They do not give up easily. They also run the minister.
This proposal is ridiculous. It was described by somebody as fraudulent. Let us call it what it is, a roaring farce. In this battle to control the power brokers in the civil service, they have more cards in this poker game than you can shake a stick at. Ministers come, ministers go, but they stay on forever. They decide who gives up. They decide who from the outside comes in.
They pretend to this House that by setting up a super ministry to guide economic problems and giving the power to advise, an amendment will be made to that order in council. I know the amendment that will be made, and so does the Minister of Finance. The order in council can be amended in such a way that it will cause a real battle.
This is not even a threat to the Department of Finance and Treasury Board; it reads "shall advise". I remember writing legislation, when I was innocent, giving the power to the National Energy Board to advise the minister. The minister never got any advice from the National Energy Board. I asked why. What I got from the officials in the minister's office, in that case energy, mines and resources, was that those guys did not know enough about it. There was not a single man in the department of energy who knew anything about energy. However, the administrators, the top mandarins, knew what would happen. They did not want advice from the National Energy Board.
We are not the only ones being taken. 1 got taken in a very elementary manner. I thought when you said "shall advise the government" it meant put in the advice and it will be accepted. However, that does not hit the root of the problem. The power has to have some core or centre, either an individual or a small group.
What we have in Ottawa is a small group of six or seven which controls the decisions of the federal government of Canada. They do not see any rivals in this present cabinet. In fact, I suspect they do not think there will be any rivals when

we form the government. They intend to run the show even after the government changes. It will be quite a battle.
In 1959 we had enough guts for a central theme on financial direction to take on the civil service. After 15 long years in opposition, we have ourselves steeled up sufficiently that we will take them on this time as well. The only difference is that this time we will know how to tackle them, matching their cards with higher cards and matching their people with stronger-willed people. The war will be won by the type of person put into the cabinet. We will see whether we can move the power from where it is now in the civil service back to the elected representatives.
We may make mistakes, but at least they will be our mistakes and we will be responsible for them. There is more than one reason why I hang around this place. I fought the battles for a few years. I lost more than I won. I want to live long enough to sit on those treasury benches just to take another crack at them. I want to see whether the elected representatives have enough backbone to win this battle.
I know these people have to learn something, and know something about something, because you are dealing with some of the most able men you could deal with. This problem exists in every country in the world. However, I want to see this job tackled in my country. I do not think it will be done with this legislation. In fact I know it won't. It will not be done with this government. It lost the will to fight before it was born in 1963. I hope that after a sufficient period in opposition, about 15 or 30 years, they will have the opportunity to recruit the type of people who will sit down, study and learn something, and then be able to do something about it when they are elected. By that time we may have the country back in shape.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to speak on the very important motion before the House this afternoon. The creation of the Board of Economic Development Ministers, under the chairmanship of my colleague the new minister of state, is a logical step in the redirection of our economic priorities. The focus of this new body will be on the co-ordination of federal policies and programs directed at economic development. This is an important initiative; it will help considerably in achieving what I have been calling for in the last year, and I support it.
As a former minister of industry, trade and commerce, and as a member representing one of the lagging economic regions of Canada, I am the first to appreciate the significance of this new approach.
As Minister of Finance, I have been very conscious of the limitations of the traditional policies for demand management.
I have explained many times that demand management policies and income policies alone will not by themselves ensure the economic performance which Canadians want. We also need structural policies which will create the right climate for the improved effectiveness and efficiency of the market. This in turn will lead to greater economic growth and to more jobs. This has been one of the key messages of my budget statements, and I think it bears some repeating in today's debate.
December 14, 1978

1 would like to give some examples of what 1 have in mind when I talk about structural policies and programs. I mean those which are directed at labour markets, at the industries that might be affected by the trade negotiations, at regional development, at the problem of government regulation, at the large tourist deficit, at our difficult energy problems.
I have also noted the importance of structural change in two discussion papers on Canada's medium-term prospects. Hon. members will recall that last February I issued a paper entitled "Canada's Economy-Medium-term Projections and Targets". That paper was basically a medium-term analysis of the aggregate components of economic growth. It recognized that broad economic conditions are a vital factor in determining our prospects. But it emphasized that a favourable medium-term economic performance would be a great deal more certain if other supporting policies were implemented which encouraged investment, improved efficiency, or helped the current account of the balance of payments.
In February, it was difficult to tell how rapid the progress would be in integrating policy approaches in these areas, or in developing innovative policies for specific sectoral problems. 1 believe that the creation of the Board of Economic Development Ministers is a major step in answering that question.
As Minister of Finance, 1 will continue to be concerned primarily with the performance of the economy at the aggregate level, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) explained when he announced the creation of the board. But I have repeatedly called for structural policies that support the economic recovery, so I am very pleased that the new President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) will devote himself entirely to putting these policies into place.
It should be clear from the examples of structural issues I have just given that their successful resolution requires the co-ordinated input of several departments of the Government of Canada. 1 look forward to working with the new minister of state on these matters.
I have also noted several times the need for consultation and co-operation with the provinces and with labour and business. As hon. members know, this is a task in which I have been engaged quite extensively, particularly before my recent budget. I will continue to consult widely on what the government's fiscal and monetary stance should be. I think it will be most helpful to have the new minister of state looking after arrangements for ongoing consultation in matters of economic development.
In his statement two weeks ago at the conference of first ministers on the economy, the new minister of state emphasized that few people want rigid five or ten-year economic plans or detailed scenarios for the future. He did not promise a single industrial strategy. I made the same point in my recent budget speech when 1 expressed my scepticism about the search for a single grand industrial strategy in a competitive market system.
Economic Development
I said that we can and must have a set of sensible industrial policies designed to provide a healthy framework for all industries and specific incentives tailored to particular needs. I applaud the setting up of a mechanism which will allow federal ministers to concern themselves with such issues in a co-ordinated and systematic way.
My budget statements have all been centered on, first, general fiscal measures such as the reduction from 12 per cent to 9 per cent in the federal sales tax and the increase from $250 to $500 in the employment expense deduction announced in my November budget. Second, I have included measures designed to improve the climate for business and investment, such as the investment tax credit. Finally, I have taken into account the special needs of our regions and of our industrial sectors. Such measures are illustrated in my recent budget by the different regional rates for the investment tax credit and by tax measures helpful to the mining industry.
The new minister of state himself explained last week that his board would review the economic development proposals submitted by program departments-and I quote:
-through one perspective that has three parts: how proposals support economic growth in Canada's regions, in industry sectors, and in the general economy.
I believe that the new Board of Economic Development Ministers will provide the knitting together of the government's broad, aggregate economic policies with its specific structural policies. This is a very important undertaking, as 1 have been saying since becoming Minister of Finance. This approach to economic development has been evolving, in fact, since the beginning of the anti-inflation program three years ago.
As decontrol is becoming widespread through the economy, it is quite timely to pay particular attention to structural problems and policies. I believe the goals of the motion before the House are the right ones in this government's program of providing more jobs, less inflation and a greater balance in our country's regional economies.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to endorse the resolution before us today for a number of reasons. First, because the establishment of the Board of Economic Development will permit me to achieve what I have wanted to achieve since becoming Minister of Finance. I have explained on a number of occasions that the traditional fiscal and monetary levers will not be sufficient by themselves to set the economy back on a recovery path as all Canadians want.
The problems in key areas such as economics, energy, regional development, government regulation, the labour market, multilateral trade negotiations and their industrial impact, have become too complex to expect that general policies of demand management will solve these problems adequately. My budget speeches have emphasized this theme. In my April budget speech, for example, I spoke of a structural reform challenge and I emphasized the progress we have made in regulating tourism, fishing and agriculture.

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
I also had two important studies published dealing with our medium-term prospects which show clearly that success stems not only from a wise policy of demand management, but also from sustained attention to the specific problems of certain regions and certain sectors of our economy. That is why, my last budget includes, for instance, measures to help the pulp and paper industry and increase, from 10 to 20 per cent, the investment tax credit in the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe Peninsula.
As Minister of Finance, I must above all be concerned with the over-all fiscal and monetary policies. I can only agree when I see that my colleague, the new President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras), will be able to devote all his time to ensuring that the proposals of the various departments in economic development matters are consistent with the fiscal and monetary policies of the government. I am convinced that the new Board of Economic Development Ministers will be of considerable help to the government in increasing the number of jobs for Canadians, reducing inflation, and better distributing our economic activity among the various regions of the country.

In some speeches hon. members have questioned what the relationship between the board and the Department of Finance will be. I do not see any problem. I think it is very important that the different departments be able to work in order to implement the structural changes they want to put forward. Very often one department has to concentrate on the problems it has to face. Such problems relate to energy, industry, trade and commerce, regional development and so forth. Sometimes there has not been enough co-ordination in developing policy and in making sure it is co-ordinated.
I worked with my colleague when he was president of the treasury board. I am used to working with colleagues. It used to be that the minister of finance was the president of the treasury board. Those portfolios were split up. I worked with two different ministers of finance when I was president of the treasury board. As Minister of Finance I worked with my colleague when he was president of the Treasury Board. Some might have said that at times the two organizations held different views. Of course, that is normal, but we always managed to sit down and talk problems over. We always managed to be in agreement when we were together in the cabinet.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) says that bureaucrats do not listen to ministers and that we are always changing ministries. I have been a minister for almost 12 years.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Good for you.

speechtext:
I know how bureaucrats operate. They give us good advice, and when we do not agree with them, they change their advice. That often happens. I held one portfolio for a long time. I was minister of Indian affairs and northern development for six years, one month, three days and two hours. I felt

no more or less comfortable in that portfolio than I feel now in the Department of Finance after 15 or 16 months. When one has been in cabinet for 12 years, one knows how the government operates.
The hon. member said we should go back. There is a kind of spirit of vindictiveness in that. I do not like that approach. Public servants give us advice, and we can accept it or reject it. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was a minister who was able to reject advice. Some cannot, but that is not the fault of the system. Perhaps some ministers are not sure of themselves, do not comprehend or whatever. Some come, some go, but a minister who wants to run his department has no problem. However, running a department does not mean a minister must reject all the advice he receives. He must be able to select from the advice he receives.
What we are doing now is making sure that in the line departments there will be a political co-ordination, under the chairmanship of the new president of the board. There will be no problem between him and me. The fiscal, monetary and economic policies will be set by me. If he comes to me to give me good advice, I will welcome it. I need good advice.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: You sure do.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Yes, and I accept it. I am not at all embarrassed by it. If I have another political minister who can look into any other department and say to the Minister of Finance, "We are having a problem in the development of an industrial strategy; perhaps we could use the tax system", then so much the better. I am not preoccupied by that. I do think the Minister of Finance has retained the same power as he had before. I see no problem. I know the opposition would like to create division within the ranks of the cabinet. If I were them, I would try to do the same thing. But I can assure hon. members that I do not see any problem arising with my colleague. I have worked with him for more than two years since I left the Treasury Board to become Minister of Finance and I have had no problem with him, nor do I expect to have any problem with him in his new job.
I do think that the new ministry will have a better political input in the co-ordination of the policies of the government. He will be consulting me. The responsibility for the budget remains with the Department of Finance, but if he gives me good ideas, I will accept them with pleasure. I am willing to do that.
So 1 do not know why hon. members on the other side are trying to see in this move a downgrading of some departments. What we are doing is to try to make the government apparatus work more efficiently. We want better co-ordination and more political input. That will be good. This will not start fights between ministers. Anyway, we have cabinet meetings all the time where we can disagree. When policies are developed, there will be some more political input, and I welcome it. I am not at all embarrassed by the move. We are just trying to do the right thing because we have said that we want to develop
December 14, 1978

the right policies to make sure that the development of the economy of Canada proceeds properly.
When I was minister of industry, trade and commerce I started this idea of having the 23 different sectors studied. And that is carried on by the present minister. That was a very positive aspect where both the management and the unions work together with the provinces and the federal government in trying to analyse and develop the proper policies for the different sectors. We said that because a policy was successful we must carry on that type of consultation. We decided we want a minister to do that on an almost full-time basis. What is wrong with that? Of course, if you are minister of industry, trade and commerce you have many other responsibilities. You have to travel abroad to stimulate business for Canada. So instead of these consultations being conducted only by burea-crats, they will be conducted by my good colleague, the new minister. I see no problem and I think it will be very good. It will be a step in the right direction.
I do not think any power has been taken away from the Minister of Finance, and if it has been, I do not mind if it is the right thing. I think that the economy and the fiscal and monetary policies of the government will continue to be the responsibility of the Minister of Finance, whoever he is.
The development of new industrial policies and the co-ordination of those policies for the benefit of Canadians can be better handled by the new board because there will be more political input. That should have been the point made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. Instead of criticizing this new move, if I followed the logic of his argument, I believe he should have been applauding it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to join in this debate, particularly after hearing what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has had to say about this proposal which the government is bringing forward. I do not think anyone denies that all governments must try to find better ways to organize their approach to the processes which they have to administer, and it is particularly interesting to look at this proposal because it brings to the forefront two important questions which we have to solve. First, how do we get a proper economic policy in this country-which, I presume, is what this board will try to do-and, second, what is the appropriate administrative way to approach the issues of economic policy-making in our country.
Everyone agrees that the complexities of government these days are great. With a $50 billion budget, no one would think a country can be administered in the same way it was administered in the past. Our modern problems are far removed from those of Sir Alexander Mackenzie 100 years ago when he was prime minister and could operate without even a prime minister's office and personally administer the most extensive ministry of the time, that of supply and services.
It is a far cry from the days of the Hon. Edward Blake who, when he was elected to parliament, was the premier of Ontario and represented two federal seats, or even of the days of Mr. Bennett who could serve as his own minister of finance, or even
Economic Development
the days of Mackenzie King when minutes of the cabinet meetings were not even kept. Those indeed are times that are far behind us.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out in a masterful speech, which I hope hon. members will take time to read with care when it appears in Hansard tomorrow and which I hope the press will read with care, some of the problems of administration as witnessed by a man who has had extensive, significant and important experience in governing. The leader of the NDP has also pointed out the problems that Mr. Wilson had as prime minister of Great Britain when he tried to find ways of administering better.
The inner story of that battle was told, as I suppose it has never been told about any other cabinet, with the publication of the Crossman diaries, which some authorities in Great Britain tried to have suppressed. However, they were published and so now all of us know more about the operation of cabinets than has ever been known by any group outside of cabinet before. What becomes so clear are the difficulties of finding new ways and structures of administering in these complicated times.
We all know the experience of the province of Ontario in the development of its policy ministeries, as well as all the experiments that have taken place in the United States in trying to find better and more efficient ways to administer. I remember when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to office that one of the members of the cabinet at that time told me that it was a refreshing experience to see a new type of administrative operation for the prime minister brought into play, a new system which he thought was going to work more effectively. I am sure that members on the government side in particular will recall the development of an extensive series of cabinet committees: the co-ordinating committees that were evolved at that time and through the last few years, the committee on priority and planning, the committee on legislation and House business, the committee on federal-provincial relations and the Treasury Board-all designed to make the government operate more efficiently. Also there are five subject matter committees: external policy and defence, economic policy, social policy, science and cultural policy, government operations, and then an ad hoc committee.
Approximately a decade later, we know the system has not worked. If the co-ordinating committees of cabinet were working, this order in council would not be before us. If the economic policy committee of the cabinet is operating, why do we need a new tier of bureaucracy in the system? It is well known that the more levels of decision-making a matter has to go through, the more difficult it is to operate efficiently and effectively. The administrative procedures put in place by the government have not worked, and consequently the government is looking for something new.
This debate cannot be as highly politically partisan as some debates. All of us must be concerned about finding a structure
2132

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
of government which will deliver service efficiently and effectively to Canadian taxpayers. I do not think anyone would suggest that our potential in terms of the resources and people in the country has been fulfilled. I am sure all of us deplore this, even the Minister of Finance and the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras). Obviously we must find a way to make economic policy work effectively.
One must ask oneself if this new board is the correct way to do it. One must look at the establishment of this board with great care, concern and considerable scepticism. The tradition of this country, dating back to the Rowell-Sirois commission when there was a centralization of authority and economic policy-making, has been that the Department of Finance establishes the economic policy of the nation. We have had the benefit of some very strong ministers of finance and deputy ministers of finance in our history. The practice has developed that the Minister of Finance and his deputy minister are the senior officials in the development of policy as far as economic affairs in the country are concerned. For the present Minister of Finance to suggest that the creation of this board will not result in a lessening of power within the Department of Finance is ludicrous. If one compares the traditional operation of the Department of Finance, one will discover that the very things the new board will attempt to do are matters which have been looked after by the Minister of Finance and his department for the last 25 years, with mixed degrees of success.
With respect, the decline in the existence of strong ministers in the cabinet of Canada came about with the co-ordinating operations in cabinet. A strong minister does not want to develop a policy which must be sold repeatedly to a variety of other ministers. The exodus of strong ministers from the government has been a product of the existing system. Also the change in management philosophy with respect to deputy ministers has been a factor in many strong deputy ministers leaving the government. The administrative philosophy relating to deputy ministers now is that one must know how to manage in order to be a good deputy minister. I agree with that. But another element of that administrative philosophy is that one does not have to know much about the substantive nature of the material one is administering. That is a mistake. Will we receive the required results if a deputy minister is deputy minister of department X on Monday, department Y on Tuesday, and department W on Thursday? Is it a good idea to move a deputy around because he knows how to manage but has no knowledge of what he is supposed to manage? We require the fixing of responsibility and authority, with strong people within strong departments, if we are to receive the type of policy the country requires.
I should like to refer to page 2093 of Hansard dated December 13, 1978, where the Prime Minister gives the reasons for the establishment of the board. He said that the board will take-
-action to influence the development of industries and regional economies-

I thought that was the responsibility of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Fessard). Surely it must be. The Prime Minister continued:
-action to integrate programs and activities providing direct support to industry-
Surely that is the responsibility of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. He continued:
-to increase effectiveness and minimize red tape-
A minister has been appointed to minimize red tape. He continued:
-action to foster co-operative relationships with respect to industrial development-
Surely that is the responsibility of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. He continued:
-direct support to industry and economic development in Canada, including government procurement policy-
Is that not the responsibility of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. De Bane)? On and on it goes. My point is a very important one. In order to arrive at good policy, we do not require another board. We require a redefinition of the line responsibilities of various departments of government.
The establishment of the board indicates that there has been a confusion in the operations of different departments. The confusion is such that they are constantly overlapping each other, with each department doing the same things over and over again. No one knows what he is supposed to do. There is no fixing of responsibility or authority.
If the government is serious about restraint and streamlining its operations, another board should not have been created. The government should have asked itself why it required another board. If the government found out that it was because of the overlapping, then it should get rid of that overlapping.
Another function of the bureau is to bring together economic policies of the government. What economic policies? Surely the departments have line functions to perform. The government knows what the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion are supposed to do within the framework established by the Department of Finance. If there is so much overlapping that the departments do not know what they are supposed to do and they have to be co-ordinated, the responsibilities of departments should be redefined in order to eliminate the overlapping so that they can operate more effectively.
The comments of the Minister of Finance were very interesting, yet at the same time they were quite shocking. He said that the board will work well because he has been around for a number of years and he gets along with the minister who will be his super minister. Surely the Government of Canada is not proposing the creation of a new bureaucracy and saying that it will work because the ministers are old friends. I cannot think of a less reasonable explanation for the development of the board. One must put forth management proposals or administrative changes on the basis that they will work effectively and last. Neither of those ministers may be there very long. The
December 14, 1978

probability is that they will not. To defend the establishment of the board on the ground that we should not worry because the ministers get along is just preposterous.
Indeed, the whole speech of the Minister of Finance on the serious issue of how we should make economic policy in the nation is a travesty, one not worthy of being recorded in the Journals of the House of Commons. 1 thought this was a serious proposal of government, but I have to confess after hearing the Minister of Finance, and it is his department that is the most seriously affected by this proposal, that there cannot have been serious consideration given to the plan.
I can tell you one thing; I would be willing to wager a considerable sum of money that if the Hon. John Turner was still the minister of finance for Canada this proposal would never have been made, because he would not permit a downgrading of his department. If it was suggested, it would not be defended on the ground that "everybody can get along with me so it is okay." Fortunately, the Hon. John Turner is not here, and I say "fortunately" meaning fortunate for the country as a whole because of what happened under his administration.
