speechtext: You very nearly slipped there.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The sort of defence put up by the Minister of Finance for the abdication of the responsibilities of his department is, indeed, something less than one would have expected. He argues that this is the way in which his sector policies are to be co-ordinated. If that is so, one has to worry a great deal about the future of the nation.
He also makes the point that the change does not matter. If I were the incoming minister of this new board I would be very worried about a Minister of Finance who says it really does not matter that we have this new board because "we meet in cabinet all the time anyway." If ever there was a statement suggesting that we do not need this board and that the taxpayers of Canada should not be asked to pay for it, that is it. If they meet in cabinet all the time anyway in a co-ordinating committee, why do they need a new bureau? Why do we have to put another layer of bureaucracy of this sort on top of the existing bureaucracy? The Minister of Finance says they all get along together in the government and it doesn't make any difference. He just laughs it off, saying "we are old friends, charge the taxpayers, it is okay with me. We meet anyway." That shows the absolute ludicrousness of the proposal being put before us.
What we really need, and need badly, is a total redefining of the line responsibilities of the departments so there is no such overlapping of functions and responsibilities. If the departments knew what they were supposed to do and knew the limits of their responsibilities, we would not need this new bureaucracy the government is creating. Indeed, what an opportunity this government has lost. It has talked of the need for restraint. If the government thought there was too much overlapping, surely there was a golden opportunity for restraint by redefining the responsibilities of departments and
Economic Development
getting rid of the confusion, rather than bringing in a board designed to co-ordinate the confusion.
Having said that, there is no question that we do need a better way of formulating economic policy in this nation. The answer clearly is not found in this sort of board, because there is just going to be more of the same input in the same way.
If we are to get the economic policy the country ought to have we have to start back in parliament. We have to start back in the standing committee on finance. We have argued as strenuously as we can that that standing committee, as is the case in almost every legislative assembly in the world, ought to get appropriate pre-budget papers prepared by the government. That committee should be able to call the most able and best witnesses from across the country. No one thinks that economic policy-making in this country is easy, and we should get all the best minds together providing input before the budget, that principal document of economic policy-making, is brought down. This committee should have some staff to assist it in its work.
It is interesting to note that the executive vice-president of the Bank of Nova Scotia made a speech two days ago, I think, suggesting that the Economic Council of Canada has outlived its function and that the staff of that council should be attached to the standing committee on finance. In that way we would have a properly staffed forum in this country in which could be brought forward the best ideas of the best economists, the best industrialists, the best manufacturers, mining people and so on. This would help not just the government, but the people of Canada as well, to get better economic policy-making than we have had in the past.
To propose that the government meets the situation by establishing a new sort of board is absolutely ludicrous. We need more openness in the making of economic policy in the country. We have the most closed economic policy-making process of any democracy in the world. We have no forecasts about what is to happen. If you were a citizen of the United States, today you would know, because the government has said, that its goal is to reduce the federal deficit in that country to $30 billion by 1981 or 1982. No one has any idea what the goal of this government is in respect to reducing the federal deficit. To have a similar proportionate deficit in this country we would need to have a deficit of $3 billion by 1981 or by 1982.
We have a strange situation here. Everyone who is considering economic policy-making and the situation that now exists is calling for reduced deficits, yet ours is going up. We have a billion dollar a month deficit. It is a deficit that is running, depending on which measure you use, almost four times higher proportionately as the deficit of the United States. This is a critical situation.
We do not need a bureau or a board made up of existing cabinet ministers, advised by the same people, to co-ordinate policy. If we are to get to the root of our problems what we really need is some place in the Government of Canada where there is someone who says what the objectives of economic policy-making are. For example, we should have someone
80067-63)4

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
declare that it is an objective of policy to reduce the size of the federal deficit. We need a place where economic policy is set in a definite way. Until that is done I am not sure we will be able to do what we ought to do in this country.
No one can object to the government trying to find a way to make better economic policy. We have had slow rates of economic growth, high levels of unemployment, increasing regional disparity of income and a devastating situation in respect of our balance of payments, to which there does not seem to be any solutions put forward by the government either for the medium or the long term.
We have a squandering of our resources, and financial controls that do not seem to have worked. We have a financial system that seems almost out of control, according to the Auditor General. We have enormous problems. One would think the government would try to find some new way of dealing with these things rather than through the creation of a new bureaucratic board. Anyone who thinks that such a board will do anything to improve the creation of economic policy in this country is deluding himself.
With all the problems before us, with the need for the development of economic policy-making, with the need for restraint and with the need for redefining the functions of various departments, how sad it is that this government has once again missed an opportunity, and once again has brought in something which has been well described as cosmetic and which will achieve nothing. We in this party believe it is not going to work. We hope that the government will not go ahead with a proposal which will do no good. It will probably cause harm by slowing down the government process and costing money. It would be better if they turned their attention to the real problem, namely: "How do we design better economic policy for this country?"

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Lessard (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite pleased to rise and take part in this debate on a resolution introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) establishing a Ministry of State for Economic Development. It is an appropriate opportunity, when we take into account the discussions held inside and outside the House over the past two years, more especially since the government paused to analyse the economic conditions two years ago. During a day spent together, the members of the cabinet discussed a new direction to be given to government action as a result of the failure experienced by the implementation of so-called traditional policies to solve unemployment, inflation or lack of investment in some sectors of our Canadian industry, more especially as far as some resources are concerned. As a result of the review of some failures following honest attempts and discussions, recommendations and suggestions made to us, after having implemented and experimented with all these policies, we were still facing, as Canadians and

as a government, a rate of unemployment and a rate of inflation which were clearly too high.
We therefore had to consider our tools for action, that is the existing laws, in order to face and deal with a situation which appeared to be of increasing complexity. That is why we had during the last two years a whole series of federal-provincial meetings in Ottawa as well as in the provincial capitals during which the federal government, together with the various provincial governments, analysed each sector of the country's economy in order to identify their weak spots, but also to come to an agreement concerning the ways to solve the problems. Mr. Speaker, after two years of concerted effort and consultation with and analyses, recommendations and suggestions from all parties concerned, we found it was necessary that the Canadian government established a mechanism for the purpose of dealing with all these recommendations from the private sector, from the labour sector and from the provincial governments.
Mr. Speaker, after some three years carrying out my duties as Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, I had come to realize that it was necessary to better co-ordinate the efforts both at the federal and provincial levels, if we really meant to reach our objective of better regional equality.
The reason I am saying this, Mr. Speaker, is to better situate myself within this debate. We heard yesterday the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) make a somewhat negative speech. We were not at all surprised, for we have come to expect from him speeches like this, and for some 30 or 40 minutes yesterday, I listened to him as he criticized us and I read again his remarks this morning. I have been unable to discover one single positive remark. I shall return in a little while to the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition, for I should like to deal now with the speech made by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). On a number of occasions, I was very tempted to applaud his remarks, and I could not help in fact applauding when he resumed his seat. The hon. member told us what he really thought had to be done by the government and I tend to believe that the ideas put yesterday afternoon by the Leader of the New Democratic Party are largely similar to those we are developing and implementing. However, it is not an easy task. That will not be achieved right away. I would even go further, Mr. Speaker. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced some weeks ago the creation of an economic development board, I was most happy. Indeed, I had written to him some months ago to inform him of my views, my orientations, how I felt it was possible to better co-ordinate our economic decision-making policy. At that time I meant to inform him of my approach and appreciation of the situation. I wanted him to know that- although I was in charge of an economic portfolio having a specific task to achieve-I was aware of the fact that I could not take up such a challenge alone-although I could count on my department, its publics servants and a budget of half a

- :v)
'pcr;

billion dollars-unless the government and other departments would make a similar joint arrangement.
We could not meet this objective, Mr. Speaker, while ignoring the other economic problems of our country and the need to develop other sectors in other areas of Canada. I cannot believe that we will lessen economic disparities by curbing development in other regions. Some people do believe that we should slow down development in some areas to allow others to catch up. I am not quite prepared to agree with this theory, Mr. Speaker.
1 think we must help all regions develop as much as possible and achieve their potential. It is only this way and by allowing potentially rich regions to develop as fast as possible that we will get the human and financial resources we need to help other regions which occasionally fall behind. It is within this context that I look at the role DREE will play as a very positive component of this new committee, this board of ministers, of that I can assure the Elouse.
In the last three years, to give you an idea of the importance of the task and of the difficulties, when I came in DREE, we began to operate under a formula called the general development agreement. We negotiated and signed those agreements with the nine provinces in Canada, as there was a completely separate agreement with Prince Edward Island. It was the result of a three-year experience in MEER which made us realize that we needed a much more flexible piece of legislation, a much more flexible working tool.
The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) opposite understands very well what I mean. I think that that mechanism is not perfect, Mr. Speaker, but it is one of the best mechanisms the federal government has ever developed with the provinces to be able to work together, to fulfil both the objectives of the provinces and of the federal government, i hear criticism from time to time both on the opposition side and outside the House, namely that the federal government, through DREE agreements, forces its own will on to the provinces, but there is nothing less true.
If I take Newfoundland as an example, where DREE contributes 90 per cent of a project on which we have agreed, we do not impose our views upon the province. We have a discussion with the province representatives and they set forth their priorities and all their needs. We examine this along with them and we indicate where we think we could join and help them. We do not impose anything upon the province. The province has the last word on where our effort will be most useful when we accept to help. So we do not impose anything. We have signed with the province of Newfoundland a long list of agreements covering all sectors of economic activity in this province. We did the same with New Brunswick. We have practically completed the whole gamut of intervention sectors in Nova Scotia and, of course, we are involved in all sectors in Prince Edward Island. We are now involved in three-quarters of the areas of economic activity in Quebec, through agree-
Economic Development
ments already in place. This is concerted action by both levels of government which want to attack the evil at the root, which want to activate and accelerate the development of their economy and particularly the resource sector.
Why is the federal government taking part in this effort? It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, since the provinces, under the Canadian constitution and the jurisdiction which is given to them, are responsible for and owners of these resources, that the federal government does not control the development of the Canadian economy 100 per cent. That is obvious to anybody who examines the situation. Since the resources belong to the provinces, are managed by them, and are subject to provincial legislation, their development will necessarily take place as and how the provinces see fit, according to their potential and the general economic outlook, both in Canada and around the world, and that is why we now have a general development agreement and we have signed subsidiary agreements in the past four years, over 100 in fact, Mr. Speaker. I have personally negotiated 80 of those agreements, and 60 major amendments to those agreements. It is no wonder that since I have been appointed head of the department, that is for three years, I have spent a large portion of my time in ministerial meetings, together with our officials, with the various provincial governments in a constant, commendable and sincere effort to help one another in achieving the common objectives of the two levels of government, namely the rational, reasonable development of the potential of each one of our provinces according to its possibilities and resources.
We signed those agreements and since its inception, Mr. Speaker, with the provinces and industry DREE has spent $3,600 billion. At this point in time, another $2 billion has been committed, money still to be paid out as a result of my own commitments or those of my predecessors-though they are largely mine for the last three years-as I was saying, over $2 billion will be paid to the provinces and industries under the Regional Development Incentives Act. To a very large extent, in fact my data confirm it, 82 per cent of my budget represents amounts committed under agreements signed with the various provincial governments in every field of economic activity.
As a result of that effort we are making together and will continue to make together we will do more together and in a more efficient way during the coming months thanks to the creation of that instrument of co-ordination. Mr. Speaker, I would not want to disclose any secrets but I am standing here with a little pride today, and more particularly today, and you understand what I mean, Mr. Speaker. Today, that board sat for the second time and today it made its first decision. So much for the criticisms made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition who said that DREE would disappear that DREE would be weakened, that its role would be less important. He said so yesterday. I am proud to be here today and announce that the first decision by the board this morning, a major

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
decision, was made on a file submitted by myself, by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and in support of the most destitute province in this country, Newfoundland, that today the government of Canada made a clearly positive decision in support of the economy of the province of Newfoundland. That is the first step.
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, and through you hon. members of this House, that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is not about to disappear. Rather the opposite is happening thanks to the experience acquired in the past ten years, the work of our officials all across this country, the rather special situation in which we find ourselves with officials in every provincial capital working on a daily basis with the people at a provincial level, the people in each of those provinces, with industry people and groups representing the workers. The officials of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion are those who are-and it is with great pleasure that I say this-are those who are best informed about local situations and who are in the best position to help this government reflect not only the situation but also the needs and projects it must support to increase economic activity in those areas. That department is doing its work and will continue to do so as effectively as possible through that co-ordination instrument.
To give you a better idea of the work they have done, Mr. Speaker, I said a while ago that we have signed more than 100 agreements. Over the last three years, and I said so in committee, in this House and publicly to the media, I tried to get the support of my colleagues. Did I succeed? Here is a little clue: out of 88 agreements signed during that period, 57 of them, from departments other than DREE, seconded my efforts.
The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources joined DREE to sign agreements with the provinces on nine occasions. The Department of Transport-and transport is very important-joined DREE to sign agreements with provinces on 13 occasions.
I have signed agreements with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce on ten different occasions. I could give the whole list. On 57 occasions, federal departments jointed with DREE to support my action and my objectives in co-operation with the provinces not only by providing the technical assistance of federal public servants, but also by providing us with millions of dollars, even though not as much as I would have liked, I hasten to add. 1 did not get as much money as I would have wished from my colleagues when they jointed in my efforts. They gave me their moral support. They gave me the support of their policies. They gave me the support of their officials, and occasionally, the support of their funds, but not as much as I would have wished.
The Department of Transport has committed $60 million in co-operation with DREE, Employment and Immigration $46 million, Energy, Mines and Resources $10.5 million and Environment and Fisheries $9 million. You can see all the money

that my colleagues have committed to my programs in addition to the contribution of DREE. All together, they have contributed $131,836,670. This is the effort of co-operation and co-ordination that I have tried to obtain and that I have been rather successfull in obtaining in the last three years. I am convinced that I have had enough discussions with my colleague, the president of the new Board of Economic Development Ministers, whom I know very well, to know what are our objectives. I can see that it is now five o'clock, so I shall continue at eight o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dan McKenzie (Winnipeg South Centre) moved:
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS WITH FIRMS AND INDIVIDUALS OTHER THAN CROWN CORPORATIONS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of all government contracts, excluding Crown corporations and agencies, with Canadian firms and individuals in the years 1976 and 1977.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I placed this motion on the order paper some time ago. The government has informed me that it is too costly and too time consuming to produce any of these documents, which number in the thousands, and we have no idea at all what it has done with these studies or whether any of the recommendations will be implemented. I would like to see many of them brought before the appropriate standing
December 14, 1978

committee so that members of the opposition can review these contracts and studies to see what they are all about. I think Canadian taxpayers are entitled to know what is in all of these thousands and thousands of contracts and studies which are costing hundreds of millions of dollars.
I have been gathering statistical information over the past couple of years through questions on the order paper, and I have only a partial count. However, 1 have information on some 940 contracts with a total assessed value in excess of $225 million. In the second stage of my study I found out that the total amount paid to contract employees during the fiscal year 1975 was $25,720,000. In 1976 the total was in excess of $21 million. The figure must be astronomical if one included the amounts for those years prior to 1975 along with the figures for 1977 and 1978.
Nevertheless I have received some answers from the ministry with regard to public servants under contract. I would like to put on the record the costs for some departments to give the House an idea of the amounts spent. Agriculture, $3,275,000; Consumer and Corporate Affairs, $1,047,000; Fisheries and Environment, $3,870,000; Indian Affairs and Northern Development almost $16 million; Employment and Immigration, $2,859,000; and Supply and Services, $959,000.
It was interesting to listen to the statement made by the new Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. De Bane) the other day. He said he believes in open government and will be co-operating with everyone. We hope, therefore, that some of these studies and contracts will be made available by his department.
I will now give some descriptions of these studies. Treasury Board spent $133,000 for a study on the psycho-social factors affecting the attitudes, motivations and behaviour of public servants. I do not know whether that study is just gathering dust on a shelf or whether any recommendations have been implemented. I think all opposition members are entitled to look at some of these documents and perhaps, some of them should be discussed in committees.
The next one I refer to is an $18,000 contract for the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to provide consultation for accurately showing canoe routes on maps. Under the Department of National Health and Welfare there is a $4,000 study to write and edit a handbook on family planning for use by pharmacists when providing information to their clientele on family planning matters. I do not know whether any pharmacists have received this or whether they use it.
There was also a study concerning the extent and level of divorce and marriage counselling services in selected communities in Ontario, for an amount of $2,000.
Under the Department of Public Works $20,000 was spent to provide fine art work for major postal plants at Saint John, New Brunswick. This was a contract given to a John Owen Cooper. I do not know who John Owen Cooper is. We should know a little bit about him and whether anything has been done with this particular study.
Government Contracts
The next one I would like to point out is a $9,500 preliminary study for a golf course at Mirabel, Quebec. As if we have not squandered and wasted enough money on that white elephant without having some kind of a study for a golf course at Mirabel. What an extravagant waste of taxpayers' money that is! I would certainly like to look at that document.
The next one is a $118,000 contract to study publicity in connection with people living on expropriated land near Mirabel in the province of Quebec. We have certainly seen enough publicity about Mirabel without giving somebody $118,000 to do yet another study on publicity for Mirabel.
This list goes on and on. I see the Secretary of States' Department with an $11,000 study to prepare design proposals for large and miniature certificates of Canadian citizenship. It also is to provide finished art work for those certificates and prototypes of large certificates if requested. I wonder where that study is today. On occasion we in the opposition get copies of these studies and contracts. They are leaked to us; that is the only way we obtain them.
The next one I come to was done by E. P. Fitzgerald and Associates in Ottawa. It is a study on the economy, inflation, housing, use of tax bonds, reducing waste in government, etc. Accompanying this study there is a letter written by Mr. Fitzgerald, the principal, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I quote from the second paragraph in the letter:
Also, at Ivan Head's suggestion I submitted the document to James Coutts for review which, owing to his crowded schedule, somewhat delayed proceedings.
I have information that absolutely nothing has been done with this document and I do not know what it cost. It is entitled "The Way Ahead," by E. P. Fitzgerald, who is an engineer. In the heading it mentions that Mr. Fitzgerald is a member of the Ottawa West Liberal Association. Are these contracts and studies being handed out to Liberal executives? Is it a pay-off? Is this part of what the Prime Minister talks about when he says in his campaigns that "there will be goodies for you"? Does he mean thousands and thousands of useless contracts just passed out to Liberal friends? Who knows? Let us table some of these studies and documents and look at them to see if any of them are worthwhile.
In this particular document by E. P. Fitzgerald and Associates it says:
The purpose of this submission is not merely to comment on the contents of the working paper, but to suggest to the Prime Minister possible ways and means of developing a more rational approach towards controlling current and future inflationary trends in Canada than is at present available.
I questioned the Prime Minister in the House about this particular document some time ago and he did not know anything about it. Here it is, we have a copy of it. Probably none of the recommendations have been implemented, but somebody has likely received $25,000 or $35,000 for it.
Here are further examples of studies, and they are very questionable. The first one is an independent study to be made in relation to the government's response to the Finkelman report; the amount is $1,800. This is going to a Macey Schwartz. I do not know who Macey Schwartz is or how

December 14, 1978
Government Contracts
Macey Schwartz was picked out to do this study, unless she is on a Liberal executive in some riding in Canada.
Here is another one "to advise on ways and means of overcoming structural problems in the government's management process and to undertake a review of the government's approach to management." The amount for this study is $6,000 and this money went to a T. Taylor.
The contract description for the next one is "to provide advice and assistance to the decentralization review group, interview departmental officials, prepare reports and make recommendations." N. B. Moyer received $22,635 in connection with that. There are pages and pages of these contracts.
The next one 1 pick out is in the amount of $12,484 which goes to a J. E. Crowe. This contract was "to advise on pensions and insurance in connection with the personnel policy manual." Maybe there are some excellent recommendations in some of these studies, but who knows? Are any of the recommendations being implemented? Does anyone know that? Is there anyone that knows just what is going on? 1 think the government ha a a responsibility to make these documents available to everyone in the House. Probably the government backbenchers do not even know about these documents either, Mr. Speaker.
I see another one in the amount of $9,600 to a C. Nicholson which was for a contract to plan, develop and undertake research projects on specific aspects of the federal statistical system, specified by the interdepartmental committee on federal statistical activities. It would be very interesting to speak to the civil servant who drafted the wording of that contract description. How he ever dreamed that one up or why we even need such a study is a puzzle to me. That one cost $9,600, which went to C. Nicholson. On and on it goes.
My colleague from Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has been the champion in fighting this government with regard to freedom of information. He is a perfect example of why we need freedom of information. He is certainly on target when we see examples like those I just read into the record. The hon. member for Peace River put out a position paper on freedom of information. I quote from it:
Hereafter follows the essentials of a program to restore some measure of parliamentary control.
(1)	Freedom of information and open government;
We do not have freedom of information or open government with regard to these thousands and thousands of contracts that are costing hundreds of millions of dollars and noboby knows what is happening to them.
(2)	Government accounting for spending of taxpayers' dollars;
There is no accounting here. We do not know anything about these documents or what is happening to them.
(3)	Need to answer for the use of special and extraordinary power taken by the Government;
(4)	More independence for private members of parliament.
As a private member, I hope to make some headway in convincing the government that some of these documents

should be made available to members of the opposition. The hon. member for Peace River goes on to say, and I quote:
Information in the hands of the people, freely available, with the exception of a few clearly defined exemptions, is essential to any democracy.
This has been going on for the past 15 or 16 years. None of these documents, studies or contracts have been made available to any members of the opposition. How are we to function properly? We have a right on behalf of Canadian taxpayers to see whether something is being done with these studies and contracts and to determine whether they were needed in the first place. 1 again quote:
Deception, lies and concealment, cover up of everything from stupid, unnecessary spending right through the erros, and corruption is the order of the day. And, because of this today, the anger, the disgust, the outrage, the cynicism, the total distrust of so many of our political institutions and leaders is frightening, but understandable.
We certainly have a classic example of that here. I have another document which was leaked to me a couple of years ago. It is an excellent study by Samson, Belair, Riddel and Stead on how the post office should be operated. I have asked that this document be made available to other members of parliament, but the government has refused.
I asked in committee why the Post Office does not implement the excellent recommendations contained in this report. I got no place at all because the Liberals and the NDP united to defeat my motion asking that we study the recommendations and implement some of them.
One of the most significant chapters in this document states that mail delivery should be left in the hands of private trucking companies. It gives dollar examples showing how the mail could be delivered cheaper by private truckers. The government completely ignored that recommendation and took away the contracting work from the independant contractors across Canada, the trucking firms, and got into the trucking business itself. That required an additional 129 trucks, 292 employees, and 105 part-time drivers. Hon. members can see the additional costs of operating the post office as a result of ignoring that excellent study. That document should have been referred to the standing committee so that every aspect of it could be studied. Hon members could have made a contribution with regard to implementing the excellent recommendations of that study.
I have further examples of these contracts. Mr. J. R. Clark received $4,000 to research and develop material for speeches given by the commissioners of the Canadian grain commission. Why on earth do we need a study like that? The government handed out $120,000 to Michael Arnold for a financial information system of higher education for federal and provincial governments. I do not know what that is all about.
It cost the Canadian taxpayers $4,950 for a study on services in a general support capacity to devise a feedback reporting system for user advisory services. Most of us would not understand that one, never mind what else is in the document. It cost $34,200 for a study on requirement contractual assistance in the area of accommodation planning.
December 14, 1978

On and on it goes. I have only a partial list of these contracts. I suggest this is something that could be looked at by the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras). The government talks about restraint and proper management. This could be a challenge to the new super minister. I hope whoever speaks for the government today will give us some information as to making some of these studies available. Maybe we cannot get them all, but possibly we can get a number of the choice ones, especially those 1 mentioned today. These should be made available to members of the opposition so that we can study them over the Christmas recess.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Harquail (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS WITH FIRMS AND INDIVIDUALS OTHER THAN CROWN CORPORATIONS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I normally start off my remarks by saying I am delighted and pleased to have an opportunity to reply to an hon. member's motion or private member's bill. However, I cannot begin my remarks like that today because I am not impressed with the position taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie).
This is not the first time we have witnessed this member take a negative position, not only in this House but with regard to questions raised in committee. The official opposition holds out to the Canadian people that it is reasonable. It tries to create the impression that it is sincere in doing its job as the official opposition. Members opposite talk about conservatism and restraint. However, this is the second time the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has come forward with an unreasonable request. I will be getting into some very specific details of that aspect.
Before getting into my general remarks, I want to take this opportunity on behalf of the new Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. De Bane) to inform the House that he will be delighted to extend an invitation to the critic of the official opposition, the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty). The minister is very sincere about this offer, and I am pleased that the hon. member is in the House so that I can seize this occasion to extend to him this official invitation.
The opposition critic and his colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, can come to the department. When they do, the appropriate officials will be duly notified that they should receive the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Duffer-in-Waterloo and his colleague so that they can be informed about any aspect of the Department of Supply and Services.
The minister has indicated to me that he is presently preparing a comprehensive reply to the letter written by the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo of December 7, 1978. The minister is quite prepared to reply to the ten points raised by the hon. member in his letter. I am delighted to inform the House that the minister will be complying with the request in the letter of December 7 from the official critic. In accordance with the policy of openness and
Government Contracts
willingness to share all available information which is not commercially confidential or which would not ordinarily be viewed by the public at large, such departmental information will be made available to Canadians.
It has been made very clear by the minister that he wants hon. members from all corners of this House to have an equal opportunity to come and be received graciously by the officials of the department. When it is deemed convenient such hon. members will be made more than welcome. Departmental officials have received and accepted this instruction from the minister, and it will be followed to the letter. As far as we are concerned, members of parliament are the most important people not only with respect to this House but also with respect to the various departments with which the Department of Supply and Services is involved.
I want to put some facts with respect to the motion before us this afternoon on the record. The department has studied this request and the size of the task outlined in this motion. I want to tell hon. members just what this motion would entail. I emphasize that the government wants to provide information which would be useful. We have tabled contracts in the past and will continue to do so within certain broad limits.
I referred earlier to commercial confidentiality. However, in our view, the current restraints on man-years and dollars would make it very difficult to comply with the hon. member's motion in the terms in which it is framed, particularly as there is still some doubt as to the purpose of the hon. members question. It is a very general question. It is not specific in any way.
All government departments issue contracts, although the Department of Supply and Services and the Department of Public Works, because of the nature of their work, are the major contracting departments.
I would like first to deal with contracts issued by these two departments, then I will speak about contracts issued by other departments.
The motion calls for copies of all government contracts with Canadian firms and individuals in the years 1976 and 1977. As hon. members know, the government's fiscal year runs from April 1 to the following March 31, and government statistics are compiled and maintained on a fiscal year basis.
In the fiscal year 1976-77 the Department of Supply and Services issued a total of 232,349 contracts and 30,662 amendments to Canadian firms or individuals, for a total of 263,011 documents. It has been determined that on the average each DSS contract contains 4.75 pages, while amendments consist of an average of two pages. In terms of sheets of paper, this becomes 1,103,658 pages for contracts and 61,324 pages for amendments, totalling 1,164,982 pages. In the next fiscal year, 1977-78, the department issued 265,305 contracts and 38,302 amendments. On the basis I have described, this represents a total of 1,336,803 pages, so that the number of contracts combined for those two years comes to 2,501,785 pages.

It seems to me that the taxpayers of Canada would have a serious objection to the expenditure of $18 million, unless there were a very defined and important objective behind the request which could not be met in a more effective and less costly way.
It would be helpful to know the true purpose of the motion. It might be that the motion flows from either a concern that the government's contracting systems are not open or accessible, or possibly from recent comments by the Auditor General on contracting in government. First, I would like to deal with possible concerns about openness in the contracting activities of the government, and in particular within the Department of Supply and Services.
Openness in the contracting system of the Department of Supply and Services is achieved through a wide dissemination of relevant contracting information to the Canadian public. This policy of openness is a further good reason why the requested contract documents need not be tabled. In order to understand fully how openness with respect to contracting information is achieved, it is first necessary to understand the role of DSS in contracting, which I will describe. In addition, it will be necessary to cover the responsibilities and procedures for contracting in so far as DSS is involved. Then I will describe the mechanisms used to provide all relevant DSS contracting information to the Canadian public. I will conclude with examples of the significant benefits achieved by the current availability and provision of contracting information to the public, which will underscore the lack of necessity for tabling all contracts for the year 1976-77.
The Department of Supply and Services provides a wide range of services to other federal government departments and agencies. The department is divided into two sections: supply administration and services administration. The services administration is responsible for the distribution of the cheques issued by the federal government, including payroll, pension and family allowance cheques. In addition, it is responsible for accounting, audit and management advisory services within the federal government. The supply administration is responsible for the procurement of everything from typewriters to tanks and ships for the federal government, buying about $3 billion worth of goods and services in 1976-77 alone.
Besides procurement, the supply administration is responsible for the provision of such other common services as printing and publishing, traffic management, warehousing and distribution, and expositions. Reporting to the Minister of Supply and Services and working closely with the supply administration is the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation which is responsible for the sale of surplus goods to the public.
The supply administration's prime objective is to provide or obtain the goods and services essential to government programs at a fair and reasonable price and, at the same time, to ensure prudence and probity in the expenditure of public funds and an equal opportunity for Canadian business and industry to do business with the federal government.
Government Contracts
As I have mentioned, one of the major impediments to tabling copies of all contracts is the sheer volume of documentation. I will give a description of the contracting responsibilities and procedures in order to indicate the complexities involved which, in turn, are reflected in contract documentation.
In a general way, the supply administration operates in a similar fashion to a supply organization within a major firm in that it is part of a larger corporation, that is, the federal government, and the basic services provided are similar. However, with close to $3 billion of annual buying power, the sheer magnitude and diversity of government operations places the supply administration in a unique position with respect to private sector supply operations. In this respect the supply administration's prime objectives are, first, to obtain the goods and services essential to government programs at a fair and reasonable price, while at the same time, second, to ensure prudence and probity in the expenditure of public funds, and third, to provide an equal opportunity to all Canadians to do business with the federal government on a fair and reasonable basis.
In the contracting process, these objectives are achieved through a judicious sharing of responsibilities between the supply administration and its customer program departments. For example, a policy has been developed which delegates low dollar value contracting responsibilities to customers, and there are provisions which allow customers the necessary flexibility to conduct emergency purchasing, where appropriate. Aside from this, some aspects of services contracting are a customer department's responsibility, although the supply administration does conduct a wide range of services contracting.
Within the contracting mandate of the supply administration, the actual process of purchasing can, and frequently does, involve much more than issuing tenders and evaluating bids. It begins with the identification of an operational need by a customer department, the funding for which must be provided for in the department's annual main estimates submission.

It is worth while for us to take a look at some of the contracts let by the government, and at some of its tendering procedures. I should like to refer the House to the Auditor General's report released in parliament a couple of weeks ago. One of the very interesting findings of the Auditor General related to the entire tendering process. I raised a question in the House on the day the Auditor General's report was released, November 24. I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about this. My specific question read as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question about the Auditor General's report. As the Prime Minister will be aware the Auditor General states in his report that throughout the government, contracts of great value are given out without calling for competitive tenders.
More contracts without tenders are given out than with competitive tenders being called.
It continued:
For example, the Auditor General points out that the Department of Supply and Services alone signed about 90,000 contracts, totalling over $1,800 million, without calling for competitive tenders.
I asked the Prime Minister how he could justify this particular activity, particularly in view of the fact that it would appear to fly in the face of the government's own regulations regarding tenders. Surely the motion put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is designed to give parliament access to this sort of information, so that we know the way in which the government's tendering process has been going, and whether money being spent by the government, which is held in trust on behalf of taxpayers, is being well spent. Surely Canadians are entitled to that information. It is an anomaly, and it is something about which I will be requesting information from the minister.
In the period looked at by the Auditor General, of the contracts identified as the source, one half of them in total numbers were given out without competitive tenders being called. Approximately two thirds of the value of the contracts given out were without competitive tendering. What confidence do Canadian taxpayers have that their money is being well spent if the bulk of this department's contracting in this
December 14, 1978

area, or two thirds of the contracts, were given out without competitive tenders being called?
In the House of Commons in the course of the last couple of weeks we have debated the issue of Loto Select. This is another instance where the government rushed into signing contracts on behalf of Canadians which ultimately will cost taxpayers several millions of dollars, because the government botched its attempt to set up a computerized lottery. Members of parliament on this side of the House-during the last couple of weeks-have requested information as to the nature of those contracts signed by Loto Canada. When one recognizes the fact that the General Instruments contract had a reported face value of approximately $23 million, than surely Canadians are entitled to know the substance of that contract. When I raised the question in the House of Commons, I was questioning on behalf of my constituents and Canadian taxpayers. I was told that parliament would be denied that information because the government specifically wrote into the contract a confidentiality clause which forbade the giving out of information concerning the spending of this public money.
What possible justification is there for government to operate in secrecy when it committed $23 million of taxpayers' money? What possible justification could there be? We are left to speculate as to what the cause was. One of the apparent reasons was that the government was so anxious to get into the Loto Select program, pre-empt the $1 computerized lottery deal, and to get in there before the provinces did, that it operated in haste and secrecy. The government made every effort possible to prevent the provinces from knowing what was happening lest the provinces should get into the field before the government did. The cost for the success the government had in getting in there first, and the cost the government had for operating in secrecy, will be several millions of dollars of Canadian taxpayers' money being poured down the drain.
We do not know yet what the figure will be. We will not know until the government has been successful in negotiating its way out of these contracts. But the government has made it clear all the way along the line that it preferred to operate in secrecy, rather than share with Canadians information concerning the manner in which this money was being spent.
Other questions arise out of this particular contract. The contract with General Instrument for $23 million was given out to an American computer company headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland, without tenders being called by the federal government. This is a highly competitive field. There were Canadian businesses in the field which were equipped and anxious to bid on this multi-million dollar contract, but they were strictly forbidden. The government did not allow competitive tendering. In the past when we asked the government why it did not allow competitive tendering, its answer was that it wanted to favour Canadian companies, that it did not want a lower bid to be brought in by a foreign competitor, and that it wanted to ensure the benefit stayed in Canada. This was a case where the government signed a contract for $23 million, in secrecy. It did not allow Canadian companies to compete. Now the government finds it has so badly mishan-

My friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, put on the record a number of contracts which he felt were questionable and which he felt parliament had a responsibility, as trustee of the public's money, to investigate and hold the government to account for. Another one I raised in the House myself a couple of years ago was one in which it was discovered that the federal government was contracting out for a study to be done of public washroom facilities.
If you were in the National Arts Centre washroom a couple of years ago, Mr. Speaker, you might very well have noticed while you were in there that there were people in there with a tape recorder in one hand and a stopwatch in the other, timing the amount of time it took you to use the various facilities. This information was gathered up from various public washrooms, fed through a computer at a cost to the taxpayer of some $200,000, so they could get some indication of how long it took people to use facilities in public washrooms. This again is an example, which I think boggles the mind, that governments are capable of getting into this sort of contract. When governments operate in secrecy without public scrutiny, this sort of contract is all the more possible. Anywhere but in Ottawa a person would be arrested for hanging around washrooms watching people. In Ottawa they get paid $200,000. There is something terribly wrong here.
I also want to deal with a couple of other matters which I think are of concern as well. I raised a question on Monday in the House about a contract which had been given to the Robertson, Nickerson Groups Associates Limited. This particular group did a study on behalf of the federal government of the training of skilled blue collar workers. Again this was done at a cost to the taxpayer. We do not know what the cost was. The government does not appear to be very forthcoming in terms of information as to its costs. We do not even know when it was received by the government. But a copy of it has become available and it is clear that in the report the group condemns the government for its handling of its manpower training policies, and points out that at a time in Canada when we have runaway unemployment, with over one million people who cannot find jobs, there is actually a shortage of skilled blue collar industrial workers and we are forced to import people from abroad to fill those jobs which are available today.
Was this report freely given out by the government? Was it tabled in parliament? Was it made available to the private sector as soon as it was received by government? No, it was received through the back door. Even on Monday my office called the minister's office to ask whether it would be possible to get a copy of this report. What were we told? Initially we were informed that they did not know what report it was we were talking about; then the minister's assistant was out all morning. He was just out of the office, or out to lunch. Then finally we learned that the minister's office could not find their copy. It had apparently disappeared somewhere. Fortunately 1 have a copy of this report, and I was able to make it available to members of the House who were concerned about it.
Surely this is symptomatic of the problems we have been dealing with here. It is symptomatic of the problem my friend,

the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, wants to cure. When public funds are being spent the public should surely have the right to see the way in which that money is being spent. The public should surely have the right to examine these contracts, and should surely have the right to study the reports which are received back by the government after the tax money has been spent.
We should take a look at the broad range of government contracting procedures and do everything possible to make sure they are open and that Canadians are not just tolerated, or that scrutiny by Canadians is not just tolerated but should be invited by the government. When the federal government is spending some $50 billion every year of taxpayers' funds, we have the responsibility as public trustees to ensure that the money is well spent. We should recognize that it is not our money and not the government's money but is the public's money.
When it comes to freedom of information the principle is very simple. It should be that the information is the property of the people and not the property of government, and the onus should be on the government to justify withholding information, not on the people to justify getting the information.
I would refer hon. members of the House to the order paper. You can look, on any day, and see the number of questions which remain on the order paper, questions asking for information on contracts, about government policies, and about actions taken by various cabinet ministers. Often this information is extremely straightforward, yet these questions sit on the order paper day after day after day, week after week, and month after month. In come cases the questions have stayed on the order paper for years unanswered.
I myself have a number of questions on the order paper at the present time asking about the government's purchasing policies and how much money it spends on various items. 1 made the offer to the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) that if he felt it was too costly to provide this information, which had its genesis in the Auditor General's report, and if he felt it was too cumbersome and time consuming, I would appreciate hearing that from him and would be willing, in instances where he could justify that, to withdraw the questions. The parliamentary secretary did not take me up on that offer. He did not say that these questions were too expensive or time consuming; he just simply left them unanswered. Surely this is a classic example of the way in which the government deals with this whole question of the public's right to know the way in which the government is operating.
With most contracts and most reports, extra copies are printed. It is not terribly costly for the government to give those copies, or make them freely available to members of parliament and the public. I think the time has come when the House of Commons should be on record as supporting the right of the public and the right of parliamentarians to do that job of holding the government to account, scrutinizing the spending activities of government and making sure that every single penny taken from the taxpayers of Canada is properly
December 14, 1978

and wisely spent. If we do not take that action today, and if we do not stand up on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada, we will be letting them down at a very important time in our history.

I did get that co-operation, as I mentioned for that matter with supporting evidence, and I repeat it tonight, that co-operation is absolutely necessary and is becoming increasingly so if we truly want to reach those objectives. That is why, Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister announced the formation of the Board of Economic Development Ministers I was very pleased because I think it is a step toward the achievement of my objectives which are precisely to bring a greater number of departments and officials of those departments at the federal level, to inform them and urge them to join in the efforts we are making to develop remote and isolated areas, those that in the last decades did not have the same degree of development as the rest of the country. And I was saying that in that effort, on the other hand, we should not lose sight of the need to co-ordinate our efforts in terms of our economic and industrial policies to make sure that the more aggressive parts of our country will continue to develop at their normal pace.
I also referred to the understanding of the former president of the Treasury Board and the new minister who was assigned the task of presiding over the board, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Andras)-I think we both have a good understanding of the objectives the Prime Minister wants to see us achieve as a result of the establishment of that board. Opposition members can attack that government proposal all they want, see it as a division, try to see a downgrading of certain departments, of their autonomy, well, to them I say this: I think Canadians as a whole want better development, a faster and orderly development of Canada's economy, more wealth and more jobs.
If certain departments have to co-ordinate their activities and forgo a certain part of their autonomy, and if this is the price we have to pay, I suggest that the price is not too high. I believe we would be making very few concessions, and then mostly as concerns our pride, by accepting to sit with five, six or seven other ministers or departments to co-ordinate our activities aimed at supporting Canadian economic development.

[Mr. Lessard.l
ture and the Department of Fisheries and Environment which in his mind should have been part of this board. It is therefore very difficult to reconcile the arguments put forth by the Leader of the Opposition who, on the one side, says that this body wields too much power and on the other side, that he would like to see other departments included in this board.
Of course we could argue extensively over the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition but I think I will content myself with these few comments simply to conclude that perhaps the Leader of the Opposition will be in a better position to judge during the coming weeks and the coming months the actions and the decisions taken by the Board of Economic Development Ministers. We have to take very specific actions which will even match certain suggestions made this afternoon by some hon. members opposite. We are conscious that if we want to implement these recommendations which number more then 800, probably half of them have already more or less been applied within the system. The 800 recommendations have come out of the 23 sectorial studies by a very broad selection of financial, industrial and labour leaders and representatives of the various levels of government during these past 12 months. These tasks force have dealt with 23 sectors of our economic activity. These people have made a great number of recommendations.
How can we expect the government to be able to implement all these recommendations if there is no mechanism for consultation and co-ordination, in order to study them and try to estalish some form of programming because it is quite impossible to implement them altogether at the same time. One must therefore provide for a gradual implementation of these recommendations made to us. Priorities will also have to be established in this gradual process for the implementation of these programs and these new formulas. That will have to be done by working closely and consulting with the provinces. All of that calls for a group of ministers to fulfil this task, this responsibility of conveying regularly in order to review these recommendations, to check and experiment as deemed necessary. We need that mechanism, and that is precisely what the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is giving us. He indicated he was going to do so by setting up the Board of Economic Development Ministers.
The hon. member of the Social Credit Party of Canada who spoke yesterday said that, in short, that board was a panic board. I shall not dwell on that at any length. In no way is it a panic board. It was set up after considerable thought, to solve a problem to meet a need. Rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that we shall not act under the stress of panic. We know what our objectives are. There are policies on which we will have to pass judgment. There are interventions the Canadian government will have to make in several sectors of the economy in coming months and years. Those interventions will be well thought out. There is no question of panic here. We will have to make decisions, and recommendations to the right hon. Prime Minis-
December 14, 1978

ter and the cabinet on what we believe the decisions should be. The departments will be responsible for delivering, implementing, applying and developing the decisions of the cabinet. That is how it will operate. It will not be a department with 2,000 or 3,000 employees as has been suggested in some quarters.
The department will include a maximum of 150 employees selected in other departments and, as a result of some consultations, there will probably be some DREE officials who will join that team to make sure that the purposes and objectives of DREE are well reflected in the decisions which that board will be led to take. Indeed, there is nothing improvised in the announcement made by the Prime Minister three weeks ago. There is absolutely no improvisation and it is merely the normal result of a development, of discussions which have been going on for two years in the country and in this House, and especially during cabinet meetings.
I see that the time allowed to me, Mr. Speaker, will soon come to an end and I would like to conclude with some more specific comments and more especially ask the members of this House and Canadians generally for their co-operation, because I think that Canadians are interested in the debate, realizing that there is an opportunity to take up the challenges they are facing.
Personally, I shall willingly work within the board with a wide open approach. I am not limited in my outlook, I am not prejudiced, I would quite simply examine these proposals. I would like to examine the segments of our Canadian economy. I would like in particular to see how the development of each segment can be integrated with the stepped-up development of the so-called underdeveloped, or not adequately developed areas. Such is my department's role, and through you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure the House as well as every province and municipality, but provinces especially, and also the various groups and industries throughout Canada, whether in Newfoundland or Labrador, northern Quebec, northern Ontario or northern Alberta, that in pursuit of our goal we will consider the particular needs and above all the potential of each of those areas, because there is a vast potential in the vast northern parts of each of our Canadian provinces. As a Canadian government, I believe it is part of our responsibility to ensure that the road we have been and will be covering, especially during the next few months, is consistent with the need for balanced development in the economies of each of our regions.
In conclusion, I would ask my colleagues in this House to support the motion put forward by the Prime Minister. It is totally non-partisan, it reflects the commendable will, and this of course will be perfectly understood, of this government to achieve in co-operation with provincial governments a more rational development of this country's potential for the benefit of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I was not able to follow the minister's eloquent address in his native tongue because I am sure it would have been more interesting than hearing it through a translation. 1 have seldom heard him so worked up or so eloquent-and in such an ignoble cause. The hon. gentleman was doing his best in a cause which he knows is lost.
When I look at this order in council, at this economic management board, I think of the old program "Superman" we used to hear on radio and read about in the comic papers- today it is a movie. "Is it a bird? Is it a plane? No, it's super-Andras." Or shall we shorten that in the future and say it is super-ass? What a confession of utter failure and economic bankruptcy on the part of the government that it should now, in the fifth year of its term, set up an economic development board under a president! It is an admission that all through its term since 1974 the government has failed in the area of economic development. Even the admission to the economic development ministers of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), from our ranks, did nothing to redeem the failure they have been experiencing for the last five years.
I know this is not an exact quote, Mr. Speaker, but the saying is that in that in the valley of the blind the one-eyed man is king. Well, the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras), the hon. member from the twin cities, the one-eyed man, is the new president of the board and in the valley of the blind he is king. The others are blind, they cannot see, they have failed utterly to accomplish anything. So they will be further ahead with a one-eyed squinter than with the seven ministers who have held those portfolios over the last few years.
Before I get launched on this address of mine, let me give you a quotation from Khrushchev. I am going right to the source, Mr. Speaker-the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) would tremble with delight were he to hear this quotation from Khrushchev who is very dear to his heart. Khrushchev once said, "Economics is a subject which does not greatly respect one's wishes." That is what has been happening in the last four or five years. The government has wished that it was competent in the economic field but economics does not respect one's wishes. Mr. Khrushchev found that out in Russia, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is finding it out in Canada. Indeed he has found it out, and now in the last, desperate extremities of his reign he appoints this superminister of economics.
I want to give several quotations at the start, Mr. Speaker, so that you may get the flavour of my address. W. C. Fields once said "The cost of living has gone up another dollar a quart." I wish the leader of the New Democratic Party were here tonight to hear something that would appeal to him, but he won't stay to hear anybody speak but himself. He gave us a lecture yesterday on the planned economy. Under a planned economy, said Mr. Carey McWilliams everything is included

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
in the plan except economy. That is the kind of planned economy hon. gentlemen to my left would give us if the people of Canada were so desperate or so down in the dumps, or so abysmally dismal in their outlook as to give that gang in the corner their vote.
Finally, my last quotation-from now on it is going to be pure me, Mr. Speaker. It is from George Bernard Shaw. Mr. Shaw said that "if all economists were laid end to end"-my God, what a lay that would be-"they would not reach a conclusion." That is what we have got here tonight. The government has been laid end to end. The ministers of the government have been laid end to end. The people of Canada have been laid end to end, and the government has not yet reached a conclusion.
I do not want to be critical. Have you ever noticed how every time this government gets into a little bit of difficulty, it adopts a change in nomenclature? The minister of employment, the gentleman who the other day was referred to as being "cullenized", was once the minister in charge of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. They changed his title to minister of employment. It did not mean the employment of one more Canadian. The status of unemployed Canadians never changed one iota because the minister has his title changed from minister of unemployment to the minister of employment. Every now and then this government wants a little name change.

What they have done this time is set up another minister. It is the old shell game. How many peas are under the shell? Under which shell is the pea? We are getting "pea'd" off with this government. We know what shell the pea is under. They do not have to carry on this shell game any longer for us. We know what the end result of that game is.
This is the emperor's new clothes policy. Do you remember the old fairy tale of the emperor who wanted to change his clothes? He was persuaded that he had clothes on, that he was looking beautiful. When he walked down the street, he had nothing on. He was naked as a newt. This is the emperor's new clothes policy. Whenever the government is in difficulty, its members change their clothes. They try to persuade us they have clothes on when they are naked. They have no ideas, no

policy, no action, no follow through, nothing. They are naked. This economic development board is the emperor's new clothes.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Hear that, Monique? Naked government!

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I did not know the hon. minister was here. I would not have mentioned that word naked.
Let us look at industry, trade and commerce. This is one of the departments that has been decapitated. It has had its head removed by the new economic development board. You might ask why that department should have its head removed. The answer is because the head has been so ineffective it might as well be removed. No wonder the Prime Minister set up this economic development board.
On November 9, 1977, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) stated, "We are on threshold of tremendous growth." I do not know where he was sitting. He must have been sitting on top of the deficit. The deficit had tremendous growth, but Canada did not. As a forecaster, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who is supposed to be one of the super powers in the economic ministry of the government, does not get full marks.
On October 5 of this year he stated in Sarnia that the Canadian economy is entering a period of stable growth. The Canadian economy went from tremendous growth to stable growth. At least that was something. Now we are in a period of stable growth. This is the same gentleman who said he favoured leaving the dollar at 90 cents U.S. He said par is 90 cents. When you have a Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who says par is 90 cents, no wonder you have to set up an economic development board. I always thought that par was 100 cents. The fall of the Canadian dollar has been useful, he said on November 9, 1977, and he hoped it would stay around for awhile. He was an accurate forecaster there, Mr. Speaker. It certainly stayed around. It is down to 84 something today. It should be 90 cents.
On May 12, 1978, the minister was quoted in the Winnipeg Tribune-he did not realize anyone read that paper-as saying he thought it would be obvious that the economy had picked up a great deal. Has anybody noticed this great pick-up in the economy this fall? I do not think so. We have noticed that the Prime Minister in his extremity set up this economic development board, but the economy has not picked up a great deal. All that has picked up a great deal is the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers. He has picked up a great deal, but we do not know how long his great deal is going to be picked up. I do not want to spend too much time on industry, trade and commerce, although I am the critic of that department.

speechtext: You mean you are going to quit reading my speeches?

December 14, 1978

when he was in our caucus. He has kept that trait. I am now looking at a CP clip which appeared in the November 13, 1978, edition of the Montreal Gazette. It contains a quote by officials of the Science Council of Canada, Mr. John Orr and Mr. John Shepherd. They stated:
Industry Minister Jack Horner is deceiving Canadians into thinking Canada has a healthy trade picture by deliberately misreading our trade figures-
A study that the minister had prepared by his department was completely a snow job because he was trying to pretend that Canada does not have a problem in manufactured end products. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce often refers to this $ 11 billion deficit and says we do not have a problem.
They further stated:
-the real weakness in Canadian industry is in the area of fully manufactured goods.
Do you know what the minister said in response to this reasoned criticism from the Science Council of Canada, with members who are appointed and paid by the Government of Canada? The minister said they are talking balderdash. He said. "What do they know about running a business in the real business world?"
While he has been here for the last 15 years agitating in Ottawa, and now springing to fruition in his department-

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Twenty years.

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. John Orr is a successful consultant and Mr. John Shepherd a successful entrepreneur, a manufacturer, a leader in the field of electronics. For the last few years he has been trying to serve Canada on the Science Council of Canada. However, they are not listened to by the government. The minister says they talk balderdash. What do they know about running a real business?
The government is not totally hopeless. On November 20 I asked the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), who is in charge of GATT negotiations, pipelines and so on, a question. I pointed out that between 1970 and 1976 Canada's share of the world market for manufactured goods fell from 6 per cent to 4.7 per cent. At that time the world demand for world exports was increasing rapidly. I asked whether he agreed with the analysis of Mr. Shepherd and Mr. Orr that a real weakness was in the area of fully manufactured goods, or did he think that was balderdash. The Deputy Prime Minister replied:
No, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that these statements are balderdash, even though when repeated by the hon. member they have not improved in transmission. They are serious views which will be taken into account by the government in its ongoing effort to develop and implement an industrial policy in Canada.
The Deputy Prime Minister had to repudiate the silly statement of his own Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. No wonder the government had to set up an economic development board.
The Prime Minister is never ready to admit a mistake. One of his greatest mistakes was admitting the hon. member to the portfolio of industry, trade and commerce, where he has listened to no one who knows more than he does. He insults
Economic Development
them all when they offer him an opinion. I cannot use up too much time dealing with the minister. I quote from a Canadian Press story of November 8, 1978, referring to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce:
He told reporters his grand design for industrial development during the next few years is to prepare Canadian companies to be ready for the major developments ahead. He offered the Alaska natural gas pipeline and the hydroelectric power project on the lower Churchill River as examples.
When asked how he knew his new approach would work, he replied, "Because I am in charge". Now he is no longer in charge. The President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers, thank God, has been put in charge.

Then one of our main economic ministers, the same industry minister, said as reported in the Globe and Mail of November 8:
-the economy is posed to move ahead strongly "if our biggest purchaser, the United States, can only get its economics right."
Imagine the gall and the audacity of that statement coming from this government, which has led this country into its present economic state, its huge unemployment, its tremendous inflation, its big deficit on the current account, its deficit on the capital account-
