-and its deficit in thinking. We will be all right. "We are posed to move ahead strongly if the United States can get their economics right." Imagine! No wonder the Prime Minister was driven to setting up an economic development board. The minister said that to the ten provincial ministers who were gathered to discuss, with him, the future of manufacturing. Manufacturing has no future if this government stays in office.
Then let's look at their record in tourism, which I mentioned in the question period the other day. We just had the biggest deficit in nine months that we ever had in our whole national history in tourism, $1,387 billion. The total deficit last year was $1,641 billion, more that Canadians spent outside Canada than people from outside Canada spent in Canada. What did the minister say? What did the minister say when he spoke on February 27, 1978, to the Liberal convention here in Ottawa? We know that Liberals will swallow anything. They certainly swallowed this one. He said:
Canada should come awfully close to balancing its tourism budget this year after two years' deficit-

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
No wonder the economic development board has been set up. Let's hope the president of the economic development board levels with the Canadian people, not with this kind of nonsense, not with this kind of foolish optimism, not with this kind of negligent, silly statement that was made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. "We are going to come awfully close to balancing our tourism budget," and we have had the worst nine month deficit ever in our history, $1,387 billion. It is going to exceed next year. The total nine month deficit was $53 million lower the year before. What does the government do to try to overcome it? The government introduces an additional tax on people who travel by air. The minister should have resigned when that tax was introduced.
The minister had been speaking to tourism groups all over Canada about how he was going to reduce costs and introduce promotion measures and all the rest of it, when our travel costs have risen higher here in Canada than anywhere else since 1971, and our tourist visits from the U.S. are down 1 per cent this year, and so on. Then the minister permitted the government to increase the air transportation tax from $8 to $15 in Canada and $8 to $12 or $13 from outside Canada. That is what he is doing. That is what he is permitting the government to do to encourage tourism in this country. He had the gall last February to tell the people of Canada that we are going to come awfully close to balancing our tourism budget. My God, no wonder there is going to be an economic development board set up to stop this kind of nonsense, this kind of ridiculous forecasting.
The government will not even consider an industrial strategy. They are too big, they are too important, they are too all-wise, they are too all-seeing even to consider an industrial strategy. They have been in power now since 1963, and still without an industrial strategy. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said in his budget speech, page 7:
I am frankly sceptical about the search for a single grand industrial strategy in a competitive market system.
I hope that the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers is going to ignore these micro murmurings from the Minister of Finance that he does not want a grand industrial strategy. Surely a look at the figures will show that we need some kind of strategy here in Canada to help develop our manufacturing sector.
I can speak for at least ten to 12 hours just on the material given to me by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, with the silly statements he has made since he was appointed in the fall of 1977, but I will just give that as a few examples and move on to this economic development board, so-called. Either this board is a nothing, either it is a camouflage, it is a piece of sleight of hand, it is a shell game, it is the emperor's new clothes, or it is something, and if it is something, if it means anything, it is a devastating indictment of the incompetence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), and all the rest of those ministers for the last four years.

If it means anything, it is an admission by the government of a total lack of success in developing our economy in Canada in the last four years. If it is not that, if it is not an indictment of the government, then it is a nothing. It is meaningless. It is what the Prime Minister called it in his speech yesterday after coming back from France, that specious speech of nothingness, the gobbledygook, bureaucratic nonsense, Privy Council colitis, or whatever it was that he made here yesterday. Bureaucratic twaddle!

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to be able to follow the type of performance we have just seen. I think it was marvellous that we could be entertained so. Like the hon. member expressed regarding the speaker previous to him, I wish I could follow him in his own language as well. I think the member is trying to create a new language for himself. He has come up with interesting words like "twaddle" and "bureaucratic colitis". There is certainly a new language coming forth. He is doing a magnificent job in entertaining the members of this House. Perhaps

the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation might find him useful in one of its comedy programs.
This was the first time I sat through one of the hon. member's speeches. I must say I was entertained. But I am very concerned. I do not believe the hon. member addressed the problem before us. He did not address the problem of planning, and he did not state his position on the concept of planning which the government put before us today. We see problems with what the government has put before us today. As most hon. members would know, we are committed to a concept of planning. We feel planning is essential to the well-being of the economy of the country. It is essential to set priorities on a national scale so that public resources, and perhaps some private sector resources, can be allocated to areas which need them the most and areas which can be most productive.
The lack of planning on any national scale has given us the present situation. Our dollar is in terrible shape. Inflation is running at close to the double-digit level. The regional disparity situation has not improved over the last ten years, and in fact may have worsened. Unemployment levels are becoming higher and higher. In my part of the country the real unemployment figure is approaching 30 per cent. This 30 per cent figure takes into account the real unemployed. This was supported this week in the figures released by Statistics Canada indicating that there was a huge number of hidden unemployed in the country to whom the government has not addressed itself. These people are being left to the welfare rolls and their own resources because the government refuses to pay attention to them. This entire situation is caused by a lack of planning and a lack of economic priorities on a national scale.
We welcome any approach by the government to plan and set priorities. We wish the proposal before us today was such an approach, that there was some real planning involved, and that it was a commitment on the part of the government to real economic planning. What is the evidence? We see the mechanism the government has put before us as a super ministry. The hon. member who spoke previously emphasized that quite well. But the problem is that there is no overriding priority given to the planning process. There can be conflict between the planning department and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). When the Minister of Finance presents a budget, he does not have to abide by the plans set by the Board of Economic Development Ministers.
Can we expect this situation to be different from the experience of Great Britain? Approximately 15 years ago that country set up a similar type mechanism for economic planning. After three or four years it found out that the mechanism just did not work because the department of economic planning, or the similar body in Britain, did not have the overriding authority to set an economic plan for the country or to make sure government policy adhered to it.
We believe a commitment to planning is important. Many structural changes are needed in the economy of this country. A good example of how planning can cause structural change in a beneficial manner is the fishing industry in Newfound-
December 14, 1978

land. For years fishermen were telling their sons not to get into the fishing industry because it was no good, there was no money in it, and that they should go to Upper Canada somewhere, or to Alberta. Now the situation is changing.
For the first time probably in hundreds of years the fishing industry holds out hope of being the key to prosperity in the province of Newfoundland. The one thing that has caused the change is organization. The fishermen have organized in the last ten years and the fishermen have themselves imposed a planning mechanism and a set of priorities in that industry. That is what is causing success in the fishing industry today. We can see that economic planning does work.
Setting priorities can bring great benefits to individual sectors of the economy. We see no reason why it should not bring the same sort of benefits to the economy as a whole. It is important to set priorities. If we do not set priorities we get a crazy sort of situation like we had in Stephenville, in my riding on the west coast of Newfoundland, where the linerboard mill has been shut down for more than a year.
At the same time as this linerboard mill has been suffering difficulties, the Export Development Corporation has invested over $900 million in pulp and paper mills abroad. Hon. members have said before that this is only investment and the money is returned, but if this country can find $900 million to invest in undeveloped or under-developed countries like Czechoslovakia, Poland and the United States of America, why in God's name can we not find a few million dollars for a mill that is down here in our own country? There are over 1,000 people unemployed because of that mill being closed down, and the whole situation is caused by a mix-up in the priorities of this government.
This sort of structural change in the fishery and pulp and paper industries, without the sorts of contradictions built in that the Export Development Corporation has precipitated, could only take place if we have economic planning on a national scale. I really question the government's commitment to economic planning when this super ministry is set up with serious defects in it. If the Minister of Finance can usurp the priorities set by that ministry, then we have seen in part the direction the policy will take.
The Minister of Finance in his budget of just a few weeks ago specifically rejected any concept or idea of planning as a way to solve the problems of the economy. With that sort of support for the economic planning ministry, how is it going to work? This just does not make sense.
That budget, as well, would have superseded any of the priorities set by the planning ministry if that ministry had been in effect prior to the budget being laid down. That budget was probably one of the most regressive we have seen in years. It did nothing, not a thing, to alter the basic structure of the economy of the country. It did not address itself to fundamental problems in the economy, the biggest one being unemployment with over one million Canadians unemployed. I guess there are one and a quarter million Canadians unemployed
Economic Development
right now when you include the hidden unemployment statistics that Statistics Canada came up with last week. The minister in his budget speech said we are going to create 100,000 fewer jobs this year than last year. What does this do for unemployment?
Regional dislocation and regional disparity have not changed at all. The budget did nothing in this regard. It probably countered many of the good efforts the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) has made over the last few years because it offered nothing to the poorer regions of the country.
There was the investment tax credit, but there is absolutely no evidence to show that the investment tax credit, over the last five or six years it has been in effect in Atlantic Canada, has had any effect whatsoever in encouraging businesses to set up in that region. That has really been a hollow sort of measure for the Atlantic region.
There are two other main problems in our economy that can be related to foreign control. Canadians do not have control of their own destiny at this time. The budget did nothing in that regard. The big problem which is really at the root of most of our economic ills is that in Canada we are digging resources out of the ground and shipping them raw to foreign countries. The budget did not help this problem at all.
The point I am trying to make is that with this sort of regressive budget set up against an economic planning ministry and taking precedence over it, how can this economic planning ministry have any effect whatsoever? Any planning would attempt to address these problems. I believe that, and I believe the super minister would attempt to address these problems in the new ministry. But, as I mentioned in this case, the budget would have overruled all his great plans.
I would like to look at the record of the government over the last few years, to examine its commitment in the past to planning even in the small areas in which it has engaged in economic planning. The planning has not been effective in solving the problems which it was supposed to solve, not even by those departments set up for that purpose. With my apologies to the hon. minister opposite, I am going to look at DREE as it is set up in Newfoundland.
There have been many dollars come into Newfoundland because of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. DREE was set up to reduce in a planned way the disparities in underdeveloped regions of the country. Speaking from the experience of Newfoundland, DREE has done much good. We have obtained schools, highways, and so on. Basically DREE has approached the problem, in its early days, especially-it has changed a little bit now and maybe the present minister is having some influence-not from a planning point of view, but from an aid-giving point of view and on an aid-giving basis. This has amounted to welfare on a grand scale for provinces like Newfoundland. Receiving aid just does not do anything to solve the basic problems.
I should like to quote from Paul Streeton, a journalist, who said:

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
Receiving aid is like making love to an elephant. It doesn't feel very good, you run the risk of getting crushed, and you don't see the results for a very long time, if ever.
That is what DREE has been. It has just been aid programs over the last nine or ten years it has been in effect. DREE was the culmination of a series of alphabet soup type programs the government set up in the 1960s. We had ADI A, ARDA, FRED, LIP, OFY and a host of others. These were the alphabet soup programs. DREE was basically the culmination of them in an attempt to co-ordinate these policies in one direction.
The concept of planning was introduced, and its stated objective was to redistribute wealth from the have provinces to the have-not provinces, structurally and on an enduring basis. That was the object of DREE when it was set up in 1969. Even though planning was necessary, DREE never moved from the aid type of approach to economic development. If you are going to change the structure of an economy of a have-not province on an enduring basis there has to be some sort of economic planning. This was never done. There were some jobs created, but not enduring employment. There is a real difference, and it is a fundamental difference to which I hope the new ministry will address itself. This certainly is not an example of how the government should address itself to the problem of unemployment and underemployment in places like Newfoundland.
There was an expenditure of mass amounts of dollars, but without planning this large number of dollars spent had a very minuscule effect upon basic problems in the economy of Newfoundland. Let me just quote some figures. Between 1966 and 1970, and 1974 to 1975, there was $185 million spent in the province of Newfoundland, which created 3,400 jobs. In its 1977 report the Economic Council of Canada said that 8,300 jobs, almost triple that number, were needed in the province between 1970 and 1975 to reduce unemployment by even one half of 1 per cent. What DREE has done, if we use the Economic Council's figures as a guide, is reduce unemployment in Newfoundland in that time period by one quarter of 1 per cent. We still have 30 per cent unemployment. Right now there are 45,000 people looking for 900 jobs in Newfoundland. It just has not worked. The DREE money has been used basically for infrastructure, which we need along with schools and highways, but it has not been co-ordinated well.
The transportation system in Newfoundland is sadly lacking. For instance, if the same amount of money had been put into the railway, Newfoundland would have a modern, upgraded railway, instead of the system it has now. Businessmen are not fools. People from the manufacturing industry would be crazy to invest in Newfoundland because it does not have a railway upon which they could depend. If the contributions by DREE to the province had been channeled in a planned way to providing infrastructure like transportation services, the province would be a lot better off. There is much that could be done, although I know that the minister is working on many things, including harbour development.

In spite of the fact that DREE, by necessity and by definition, has had to have a planning approach to its operation, it still does not work. In fact the planning by that department has even been counterproductive in some ways. To illustrate this I would like to quote briefly from the Report of the People's Commission on Unemployment at page 70:
Between 1969 and 1975 DREE spent more than 75 per cent of all its moneys in the province on what the Economic Council of Canada calls "non-rural infrastructure". What this means is that DREE's money has gone to build roads and schools, just as the west coast businessman quoted above suggested.
That refers to a previous quotation. It goes on:
The commission finds nothing wrong with the construction of roads and the building of schools. But we must seriously raise the question as to whether DREE has, through its support for urban development, made our rural areas less competitive in terms of economic development and job creation.
This illustrates that DREE, even though it has not provided substantial benefits to the urban communities in Newfoundland, has contributed in a very detrimental way to the rural areas of that province. It is fortunate for the rural areas that the fishermen's union, through its policies, is making these areas much more viable, because fishermen and fish workers can now stay in the small communities and live a good life there. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion has also provided aid to businesses in the region, but again in the absence of priorities and sound planning we must question its value. In this regard I would like to quote again from the Report of the People's Commission on Unemployment:
However, one still must be aware of the apparent illogic involved in an approach to alleviating regional underdevelopment and worker poverty which begins by giving large sums of money to those who are already well-off and who, if successful, will succeed in increasing their fortunes even more.
I would contend that Canadian development policy, to the extent that it is based on incentive grants to corporations, is trying to combat regional underdevelopment by giving money to those economic interests which are essentially the cause of underdevelopment.
Again, because there has been no sound approach to economic planning, DREE's contributions have had a negative effect in some respects in the province, and in many ways have contributed to factors helping to keep the province underdeveloped.
Through DREE the government has tried to alleviate disparity by planning. It has failed because there has not been a substantial change in relative economic welfare in the various regions of the country, with the exception of Alberta with its oil revenues. Other regions such as the Atlantic region, the Gaspe Peninsula, and so on, seem to have gotten poorer. It is the old story, the rich get rich and the poor get poorer. In light of the high unemployment in these regions, if this approach continues who knows what will happen? The unemployment rate nationally is 8 per cent. If it were 8 per cent in Newfoundland, everybody would jump for joy. Even the official rate of unemployment in Newfoundland is double that figure.
By developing the urban areas, DREE has undermined the ability of the rural areas in the province to support those who live there. We cannot solve the economic problems of Canada by planning which includes only the upper echelons of the economic society. DREE has made massive payments in Newfoundland which in many ways are responsible for the under-
December 14, 1978

development of the province. For example in the fisheries industry, it was only when the fishermen organized themselves and began developing the industry at the grassroots level that they began to see benefits from that industry in the small communities. We must re-evaluate the planning strategy and direction of DREE if we are to have any lasting benefits upon the economy in underdeveloped regions like Newfoundland.
The government's economic planning is just as bad in other areas. It has set up the department of employment, or more aptly it should be called the "department of unemployment." Its purpose was to have a planned approach to the human resources of the country, with the idea of moving people to where the jobs are. It sounded good on the surface, that people could travel from one part of the country to another. Emphasis must be placed on the word "could" as opposed to forced to move. As a result of this type of planning there has been a massive migration of young people from the Atlantic region. I can recall reading statistics some time ago which showed that in the early part of the century, up to the 1930s, approximately one half a million people had left the Atlantic provinces.
The department of employment has set up all sorts of manpower mobility programs, suggesting that people move to Ontario or Alberta, the lands of milk and honey. It just does not work that way. This plan has caused the relocation of thousands of people in this country, the breakup of many families and other major social problems. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) made some comments last week in this regard which I felt were unforgivable, but I will not go into them.
There is, however, an interesting slant to this. I am not one for reading poetry, but I would like to refer to a poem by A1 Pitman, the last line of which I have adapted myself. He is a well-known literary figure in Newfoundland. The poem is about the idea of mobility, forcing people to move, saying that the opportunities are greater elsewhere. The poem reads as follows:
Now here is the gist of this marvellous plan To save all the livyers of this Newfoundland;
Just take one half of the horrible lot And send them to pickle in Canada's pot
Take a daughter, an uncle, some sisters and brothers And put them on barges along with the others And bid them good-by and say now there you go You're going to glory in Ontario
And when you go to see Davis up there Just tell him you're looking to go on welfare Just tell him you're victims of governments' plans Invented in hell and then spread on the land
With apologies to A1 Pitman, Mr. Speaker, that expresses my sentiments exactly on what this mobility is all about. If one wants to say to half of the population of Newfoundland that they should move to Ontario, that is fine, but is not the way to go about economic development. It does not change the problem but just moves it somewhere else.
Economic Development
All the planning that is done in this area ends in exporting people. It has often been said in Newfoundland that, after fish, our main export is our young people. In all parts of the country there are Newfoundlanders working, not necessarily because they want to be in those parts of the country but because of economic necessity. A lot of them leave their families in Newfoundland because they cannot afford to take them to Alberta or wherever they go, and we all know the consequences of that.
The other creature of the department of unemployment is the Canada Works Program, which I have talked about on other occasions. On page 84 of the People's Commission Report there is an interesting comment on the Canada Works program and others like it. The federal and provincial governments were unable to conceive of a strategy of development in the province that was based on- the social and economic traditions of the people. Instead, they performed the role of subsidizing industry, either through granting generous concessions to developers who invested in the province or through using manpower training and mobility schemes to move workers to central Canada.
All we see are programs that beg the question of real economic development in the country. They are stop-gap measures, and they become important in parts of Newfoundland because they are all there is at certain times of the year. They do not solve the problem, however; they provide jobs but not real employment. This is typical of the economic planning that has taken place in the past. Atlantic Canada has been a labour reserve for Ontario and Alberta. Education ministers from the Atlantic region have complained that "we train them, you claim them", when referring to our young people. The Atlantic region has had to subsidize education, to train workers and young people with skills not used there, but that are useful in the western provinces or Ontario.
What has been looked upon as a planned approach to the economy has actually been a direct subsidy to two main groups: first, to industry by give-aways under DREE and other programs and by subsidizing and forcing the mobility of the labour force and, second, to transfer payments, which is probably the most insidious. Forced welfare programs are designed to give purchasing power to people in poorer regions, not out of genuine concern for their situation but so that they have the purchasing power to buy goods made in Upper Canada or in foreign factories. This approach solves nothing. We have to look at the basic structure of the economy. The basic defects of this new super ministry make it impossible for us to have effective economic planning. After ten years of defective planning the government expects us to swallow this super ministry with all its own defects.
On the surface there is no commitment to economic planning. Time and time again we have said we are committed to positive, effective economic planning. We would support the government if we felt the proposal was a commitment to economic planning, but there is no evidence of that. This is just window dressing. The new super ministry will have no power to impose an economic plan on our economy.

December 14, 1978
Economic Development
We support real economic planning, but we believe that implementation is probably more important. Of course there has to be a plan, but implementation is the key to success. We have developed an economic plan based on our view of the Canadian economy. It is not a complete view but is one that we feel represents an approach that would be beneficial to Canada. Of course we would like to see it implemented, and perhaps we will present it to the new super ministry in the hope that this will happen.
I will not take any more of the time of the House, Mr. Speaker. I would just like to say that this super ministry has some definite defects. Its planning potential will be muzzled by the veto of other ministries, the Minister of Finance in particular, if future budgets are as "progressive" as the budget he presented a few weeks ago.

Hen. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I want to say, to begin with, that I support this proclamation and all it entails, as one of the ministers who fully expects to profit from it.
To be blunt about it, my position, and that of other individual economic ministers, are strengthened by this move. I do not believe in working in cabinet by playing a lone hand. I prefer having allies. When my proposals to assist exports or to further support domestic industries go before cabinet, and they are endorsed by the nine other members of the board, that will strengthen those proposals a good deal. It gives them a strong leg up. Ten ministers of one cast of mind, economic growth-oriented, certainly have a tremendous influence within the cabinet structure.
It only makes sense, sir, to integrate policies that affect economic development and to view those policies as to how they impact on one another. It only makes sense, to me, to consider policies and programs from one basic perspective- how will they help the growth of industry sectors and industries within a specific sector to which they apply. How will they help the growth of the regions, the growth of the general economy? It only makes sense to bring co-ordination and over-all economic development under one roof. And finally, it only makes sense to focus in one place the consultations with provinces, industry and labour, that have taken place in the past under a variety of ministers.
I look upon this as being similar to the things I have seen in Germany and Japan. Those countries have paid a great deal of attention to their industrial thrust since the Second World War. They fully believe that industry is the engine that makes the standard of living that they enjoy possible. When one travels to Germany and sees-
[Editor's note: Whereupon a stout gentleman, dressed in red, with white fur trim, entered the chamber, exclaiming, "Ho, ho, ho!'']

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MINISTRY OF STATE FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a minister participating in this economic board, I certainly want the House to know that I am no Santa Claus.
In Germany they pay a great deal of attention to industry because they believe it is the engine that provides the quality of life they want. In order to do business you have to join the chamber of commerce in Germany; if you are on that side you have to join their industrial board. In Japan, there is a board of industry composed of senior industrialists, called the Kei-danren, and the government pays a great deal of attention to the needs of industry there. I look on this new thrust as being somewhat similar in purpose. The government is demonstrating to industry that industry is important to the economic well-being of this country. Industry will make possible the social services we all want, as Canadians, to enjoy, and which can be provided as long as the proper amount of assistance is available.
My department will continue its normal activities. We shall continue to propose policies designed to benefit industry. For example, I am launching two major consultative exercises with business and labour. One is to assess and make recommendations upon the efficacy and scope of the services and policies provided by government to assist exporters. A blue ribbon committee of business and labour leaders will be headed by Mr. Roger Hatch, president of Canpotex. Its membership is representative of our exporting industries and of our regions. I am looking to this committee for strong recommendations as to how we in the federal government, together with provincial governments, can improve our performance in supporting exports.
Some hon. members have asked why this should be done now. I think it is important that the House should recognize the reason for the action we are taking at this time. We are entering upon what will perhaps prove to be the most competitive era in Canada's recent history. The years ahead will be tremendously competitive for any industrialized nation and we must address ourselves to this task. The new ministry will, I hope, be successful in furthering the liberalization of trade.
Canada depends a great deal on its ability to sell abroad. As I have pointed out on past occasions, approximately 25 per cent of our gross national product is derived from exports. If hon. members want to relate that figure to the Japanese experience I can tell them that 13 per cent of Japan's gross national product is related to exports. In the United States, the figure is 7 per cent or 8 per cent. We have to meet the competitive forces which will be upon us in the eighties, which means we shall have to attach greater importance to the role of industry in our economy. I look upon this new departure as signifying to industry that we are there to help them and that we have the power within the cabinet to make certain that the engine moves well and provides Canada with the resources to accommodate people with the standard of living we believe they should be able to afford.
December 14, 1978

I mentioned I was going to set up two task forces. The other group, consisting of senior private sector leaders, is taking on a very important task. Its members represent a cross section of firms, both large and small, in the Canadian resource and manufacturing industry. This task force is meant to assist Canadian companies to win contracts arising from the major industrial and energy projects which are about to come on stream in Canada; it will work with and make recommendations to both federal and provincial governments.
This country is launching upon a series of very large projects worth billions of dollars. The Canadian section of the Alaska pipeline is one-it has already been mentioned in this debate. Mr. Speaker, that is worth $4.3 billion in contracts for design engineering, steel, and a host of supplies ranging from manufactured products to food, transport and other services.
Other large projects planned in the fields of electrical generation, mining, forestry, petroleum and petrochemicals over the next decade are expected to exceed in value $50 billion in construction work. These Canadian projects can provide a large majority of Canadian contracts and jobs, located, as they are, in northern Canada, on the west coast, the prairies, central Canada and Atlantic Canada. They are a vast and varied market for Canadian industry. Canadian designers, engineers, consultants and services, manufacturers and steel plants must win the majority of contracts in competitive bidding.
Without ordering the placing of contracts by government decree, without intervening in a way which would contravene international trade practices and perhaps get us into a great deal of trouble with our trading partners, the bottom line is that the large majority of industrial benefits must go to Canadians. This is important for the immediate contracts and jobs involved. It is equally important in terms of new technology, new skills, and ability to merge into effective consortia to tackle large and complex projects, all of which are necessary if Canadians are to succeed in that competitive bidding role.
The task force of the 25 business leaders and senior labour representatives working with the provincial and federal governments is charged with identifying means to ensure that we get those contracts and those jobs. It will identify and communicate in advance the opportunities which are expected so that Canadian companies may know what they should be competing for. It will make recommendations concerning procurement by governments. It will make recommendations with regard to government policies which can be supportive of the objective. It will take a look at ways in which companies pool their talents and abilities to take on new and larger tasks.
From time to time we hear members complain about imports of manufactured goods into this country. They ask what the government is doing about it. This task force will be looking at that situation to encourage the Canadian manufacturing sector to meet better the challenges of supply-to increase the supply of steel, electrical generators and other equipment necessary to the huge projects which will be started between now and the year 2000. The other task force has, of course, been set up to assist in meeting challenges in world
Economic Development
trade. This is our way of supporting Canadian industry both at home and abroad.
I am pleased that the Canadian Commercial Corporation will now be in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, which is where it should be. I certainly believe it can play an aggressive role in assisting the private sector to seek contracts with foreign governments. It fits logically within my department; so rather than losing power through the recent shuffle my department has, in fact, gained power. It is not sufficiently realized, especially by hon. members opposite, that we provide about $3.7 billion worth of support for Canadian industry every year, three quarters of which goes to encourage Canadian exports.
Some hon. members wonder what I have been doing this year. Well, the Enterprise Development Program has recently been doubled and the EDP loan guarantee ceiling has been raised from $350 million to $1 billion. We have set up advisory boards in every province to make certain that both small and large industries are aware of the assistance the EDP can give them. Some hon. members may have noticed in the papers today an announcement that the board is to lend money to establish two-way trade between Nova Scotia and British Columbia.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-FUNDING OF PLANNED PARENTHOOD ASSOCIATION
HEALTH AND WELFARE-FUNDING OF PLANNED PARENTHOOD ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight in this House unashamedly as a Roman Catholic. However, it is my fervent hope that I will always use my position to defend with equal vigor and sincerity the integrity of any religious denomination which I feel has been impugned.
As to the point in question, on November 3, 1978, as reported at page 771 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) if her department had funded the publication of the fall, 1978 edition of the Planned Parenthood Federation newsletter. She replied that funds from her department were used strictly for the operation of that federation's national office.
By sad coincidence, the editorial address given on the newsletter is, in fact, the national office of the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada; in other words, as the minister herself stated, the office from which the offensive missive has been
December 14, 1978

transmitted operates, thanks only to funds from the federal Department of National Health and Welfare.
I would like the House to consider for a second what is offensive in this missive. The subject of the newsletter is abortion, and it is a subject open to debate which would go on much longer than the seven minutes allotted to me. However, in my view and in the view of millions of Canadians, abortion is killing. It is the taking away of life. I will not go into that point of debate.
The point I am making is about this particular newsletter of the fall of 1978. Articles in various newspapers, mainly Canadian, by the way-the Globe and Mail, very often the Toronto Star, the Ottawa Journal and the Ottawa Citizen- are interpreted as being in favour of abortion. Among all the quotations in newspaper articles there appears one entitled "Pro life isn't". There is some recognition given to the author of this editorial. It is quoted as being the National Catholic Report of July of 1978.
A tiny bit of checking on my part-it did not take very much-proved to me that this so-called National Catholic Report comes from the United States in the first place. Despite the fact that it is national in a large country like the United States, it has a circulation of less than 46,000. By national standards that is an extremely small circulation. Therefore someone in Canada would have to undertake a certain amount of research to find that particular article. He would probably have to make a few international telephone calls.
The article in question was written by a Catholic. A little more research on my part revealed that the publication to which I referred is a Catholic newspaper, but it is written by a certain dissident group from the Catholic church and in no way-and this is the point to be made-does it respect or reflect the traditional view of the real Catholic church.
If the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada wanted to find out what Catholics think of abortion, it could have gone to L'osservatore Romano, if it understood Italian. The federation could have asked me for a translation. If the federation did not ask me, it could have gone to the Catholic Register or to many other Catholic newspapers in Canada, none of which would ever, ever have given the impression that pro-abortion people are Catholic or that Catholics do not give a damm about people who are born.
The only concern of Catholics, according to this article, would be to save the four-month fetus, and to hell with four-year old child living in squalor. That is a travesty. It impugns the integrity of every Catholic. I do not know whether the author is Canadian or American. I do not know his or her nationality, but what is the motivation? That is what we have to ask ourselves. What is the motivation for going to a very small, little read, dissident Catholic newspaper, and then printing this rubbish, this garbage, as if it were something from the Vatican?
This newsletter obviously is of no moral value at all. They do not know the meaning of the word religion. Why did they
Adjournment Debate
print it in the first place? Who is funding this publication? The minister said that federal funds were used only for the organization of the national office. We have already found that the national head office is the place from which this spurious paper emits. What does the funding do for the organization? It pays for rent, electricity, and for staff. For the minister, with all due respect, to tell me, "No, we do not fund this subliminal anti-Catholic message" is, I suggest, an insult to my intelligence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-FUNDING OF PLANNED PARENTHOOD ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking tonight on behalf of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Robinson) who is unavoidably absent.
At the start of my remarks I should like to say, in response to the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni), how much respect I have for her. I also want to put on the record, for her information and that of other members of the House, that, being a Catholic myself, I have great respect for the points she brought forward tonight. However, further to the minister's response of November 3, 1978, to the question of the hon. member for York South concerning the fall 1978 edition of the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada newsletter which, as she commented, contained "despicable and insidious innuendo which vilifies the entire Catholic church," I would like to make the following remarks.
I have had the opportunity to review this particular publication and I saw no remarks directed at the Catholic church. In the provincial-territorial news section of the newsletter-the section in which there are references to the Roman Catholic church-it is reported that Planned Parenthood Yukon has co-sponsored with the Roman Catholic parish, workshops for parents. There is also a reproduction of newspaper clippings, one from the Globe and Mail of April 25, 1978, and the other from the National Catholic Reporter of July 14, 1978, both of which mention the Catholic church.
One article reproduced from the Globe and Mail of April 25, 1978, outlines the position put forth by the Chancellor of the Roman Catholic archdiocese of Toronto which calls for mandatory instruction and testing on how to be good parents for all couples planning marriage. The other reproduced news clipping which refers to the Roman Catholic church appeared on the editorial page and was drawn from the National Catholic Reporter of July 14, 1978. The editorial states in part:
There is something wrong in the pro-life movement that causes many Catholics concerned about peace and justice-life-to look askance, or grieve about the misdirected energy. The national "right-to-life" movement isn't "pro-life" at all-it's anti-abortion. The self styled "pro-life" movement, therefore, whatever the attitudes of individual members, comes through in a single-focus frenzy, apparently lacking Christian understanding regarding life in general. There are individual pro-lifers whose cares are larger, but they are scattered, and so is their impact.

December 14, 1978
Adjournment Debate
The editorial continues in this manner.
In addition, there are 30 or more other reproductions of press clippings of Canadian and American newspapers.
As can be seen, the references to the Roman Catholic Church are contained in reproductions from highly regarded newspapers or based on material from other publications, such as the National Catholic Reporter.
For the record, I would like to make it quite clear that the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada has, over the years, constantly provided a high quality of family planning services. Associations of the type set forth by the hon. member for York South can only foster misunderstanding and hard feelings in the groups genuinely interested in promoting responsible parenthood.
In principle, the Department of National Health and Welfare does not control the content of the publication of the voluntary agencies it funds. In particular, the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada newsletter has been dignified in tone, content, and reflects responsible work done by dedicated volunteers promoting responsible parenthood.

Mr. Speaker, on November 9 I rose in my place to ask the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo) the following question:
Our own House last week passed a unanimous resolution expressing our concern for the abridgement of freedom of thought and expression in the Soviet Union as demonstrated by those trials.
In view of the upcoming 1980 Olympics to be held in Moscow, could you tell me whether there are any plans in your department to re-examine our country's position vis-a-vis participation in the Moscow Olympics?
The answer of the minister was so twisted that it looked like a pretzel. She said the following:
-I am quite prepared to accept that there be sport boycotts when related to sport, but when the matter is outside the realm of sport I do not feel the sport should be used as an instrument through which retaliation is executed.
The minister directed a letter to me dated November 10, 1978, which reads in part as follows:
-in principle, we consider that sport should not be used as a political instrument except in cases where the matter in question directly affects sport, as apartheid does.
The minister is living in an Alice in Wonderland world.
I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the November 12 edition of the New York Times. It was written by Yevgeny Rubin, a former sports writer for the Soviet Union. In part it reads as follows:
Soviet sport is a facade, or the brightest, loudest and most glaring part of the facade. Athletes-strong, agile, tanned and invincible-are supposed to person-nify the Soviet way of life to the world, including their own people. With each record, each victory, each goal, the athlete is supposed to demonstrate that the Soviet people are the strongest, the fastest and the most graceful.
(Mr. Harquail.J
If that is not politics in sport, I should like to know what it is. The minister implied that she had nothing to do with the decision, that it is the Canadian Olympic Committee which makes the decision. But she has a lot to do with the funding which goes to that committee, its grants, or the withholding of grants. All one has to do is ask Mrs. Koop whether that is the case. The incredible answer of the minister reflects her naivete. If anything, the minister has raised the concept of apartheid and not I. Since the minister raised apartheid, I will refer to it. The minister ought to know that all legal restrictions in the country of South Africa have been withdrawn from apartheid. I am not saying that it has been withdrawn in the countryside, but certainly the legal barriers have been withdrawn from the legislation.
I have seen the pain which apartheid brings. I have seen some of that anguish. I realize the pain of the hundreds of workers from Mozambique who work in the deep mines of South Africa, live in fetid dormitories, and are kept from their families for 11 months of the year. The same thing is true in Russia where people are kept in forced labour camps in Siberia, in the freezing cold of Siberia, for 12 months out of the year, and are never allowed to see their families. All one has to do is read the book entitled "A Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich" to know something about that cruelty.
I have seen some of the incredibly cruel and unjust treatment of the millions of blacks in South Africa who are not allowed to hold citizenship or own property. That is true also in Russia where the property of dissenters is seized. They are drafted into the army so that they cannot leave the country. Is one better than the other? One is just as cruel as the other. I remind the minister that pain does not recognize the colour of skin. All races in South Africa be they coloured, white, Indian or black, are made in the image of God. They deserve to be treated in dignity and with the dignity all God's creations deserve. If that is true of South Africa it is certainly true of those people in Russia who have convictions and feelings they ought to be able to express, and they ought to be able to find expression for their convictions every day of their lives.
Ask all those people we have talked about in this House how they feel about this. If the policy of detente of this government and of other western governments is designed to break down the barriers between us and the Eastern bloc countries in respect of all of those things that are repugnant in that present system, why should that policy not work in other countries where there is another kind of discrimination?
Would it be too much to ask this government just once to carry on a consistent policy in this matter? Even better yet, would it be too much to take politics out of sports altogether and allow athletes from all around the world to compete without any government controls or restrictions?
I am not fighting against Canadian participation in the Olympics in Moscow or in any other city in the world. All I am asking this government to do is recognize that pain is universal, and it does not matter whether it is in a Russian
December 14, 1978

concentration camp, a Russian insane asylum, or in a South African mine. All I ask this government is to start being consistent in its policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh A. Anderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is obviously aware that the immediate responsibility for Canada's participation in the Moscow Olympics rests with the Canadian Olympic Association and not with the federal government. The Canadian Olympic Association solicits private sector funding through the Olympic trust. In addition, funds are provided to the association by the fitness and amateur sports branch as part of its program of assistance to sports associations to ensure participation by high performance Canadian athletes at international competitions.
The need to avoid government intervention in the affairs of autonomous sport associations such as the Canadian Olympic Association is recognized and respected by many groups in Canada.
In the circumstances which we currently face regarding the abridgement of freedom of thought and expression in the Soviet Union, we do not consider the Olympics to be an appropriate forum in which to express our views on human rights in the U.S.S.R.
I am rather amazed that the hon. member should state we should keep politics out of sport, while at the same time asking whether the Government of Canada would prevent participation in the Olympics by Canadian athletes. I cannot reconcile those two statements by the hon. member.
I believe you will find, Mr. Speaker, our policy consistent with the government sport boycott of South Africa. The United Nations in 1971, 1975, 1976 and 1977 adopted a series of resolutions calling on all member states to refuse any sponsorship, assistance, or encouragement of sporting contacts with South Africa. Canada supported all those resolutions.
At this time no such international reservations exist with regard to a sport boycott of the U.S.S.R. and, therefore, in reply to the question of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen), the fitness and amateur sport branch does not believe it appropriate at this time to alter its position vis-a-vis participation in the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

I posed a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) in the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). This was on December 8, and I would like now to read that question:
Adjournment Debate
Considering the certainty of great financial loss to certain businesses such as automobile and machinery dealers who have substantial inventories on which the old 12 per cent sales tax has been paid, will the minister indicate whether he is considering some form of adjustment in the sales tax formula that would minimize the financial loss of those businesses?
The Minister of Finance said in his speech on November 16, "I want this passed on to the consumers". I speak tonight on behalf of automobile and machinery dealers and businesses with other inventories subject to the reduction in this tax. I say to the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance that this is a very cavalier and deceptive approach to this question on the part of the government.
Just because the government is almost bankrupt, that is no reason why it should also bankrupt the retail dealers of this country. When the minister says he wants to pass this 3 per cent reduction on to the consumers, his approach should be honest and fair to everyone. He should recognize that the automobile and machinery dealers of this country should be compensated for the reduction they will have to make in their inventory prices.
I have with me two good examples, borne out in letters from dealers in my riding who will suffer losses as a result of this action by the government. The first letter is from Pringle's Service Ltd. in Napanee. It reads:
Dear Doug:
I am writing you to express my deep concern over the effect the recent federal sales tax reduction has had on me as a small businessman, as well as thousands of small businessmen, like myself, all across Canada.
Although I heartily applaud the government's initiative to lower federal sales tax, albeit long overdue, the immediate effect of this change is myself being caught with over 60 new cars and trucks that are, on the average, $175 overpriced. If I don't reprice my stock, customers will not buy from stock, but rather order the same vehicle from the factory at the new lower price. But to reprice my entire stock means writing off $10,000.
As it now stands, the Canadian car dealers are left holding a multimillion dollar price tag. As a small businessman, I resent this indirect budgetary subsidization. Since the November 16 budget speech, my firm has been unable to sell a new 1979 vehicle out of stock.
I urge you to push for a 3 per cent federal sales tax rebate of instock vehicles for small businessmen like myself right across our nation.
It is signed Larry A. Pringle.
I would like to quote from another letter I received from Revell Motor Sales Limited in Verona, Frontenac County. The letter is addressed to myself and includes the copy of a telegram sent to the Minister of Finance on November 27. It reads:
Dear Mr. Alkenbrack:
Re: Budget-Federal Sales Tax Reduction.
Please Find listed below a copy of a telegram we have sent to the Minister of Finance.
We feel heavily penalized by this tax reduction as this will cost us in excess of $22,000.
I, a businessman, do not feel I should have to subsidize your tax cut.
Our customers are waiting for the lower priced vehicles and I am left with over one hundred (100) vehicles in inventory and at 12.50 per cent interest rate, I feel this is a severe and unnecessary penalty to car dealers over other retailers.
Rebates of this nature were granted in 1961, 1968 and 1974 and should certainly be granted again at this time.
2164

December 14, 1978
Adjournment Debate
As our net profit is less than 2 per cent, we feel we cannot afford this. We need your immediate attention to this matter.
Yours truly,
H. M. Revell Revell Motor Sales Limited
If the minister wants these reductions passed on to the consumer, he should give each dealer credit for the savings that he has had to pass on to his customers. It is not difficult to do.
Both the Minister of Finance and Minister of National Revenue have complained about the tremendous amounts of money and very numerous accounts that would have to be serviced. But every automobile manufacturer has a computerized record of every dealer's inventory on November 16, which was the date of the minister's announcement, and through this they have the ability to make an accurate total of tax reductions and/or rebates that should be credited to the dealer as he sells an automobile to his customer.
I appreciate that some adjustment has been made in the time of transit of automobiles from factories to dealers as of November 16, but that is not enough.
Both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue have pointed out that it would cost many millions of dollars to rectify this problem. This government ought not to have made the automobile and machinery dealers of Canada pay for this aberration on the part of the government.
I reiterate, there is a precedent for a rebate in the 1974, 1968 and 1961 budgets. Let the minister now be fair and follow those precedents.
I note, Mr. Speaker, in the proceedings of today the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) has obtained an agreement from the Minister of Finance to meet with a delegation of representatives of the Automobile Dealers of Canada, and I say let the government and that delegation work together to right this inequitable situation, and this gross example of unfair financial discrimination against a very important segment of our economy, the Canadian automotive retailers.

speakeroldname: Miss Aideen Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-SALES TAX REBATE ON INVENTORIES OF MANUFACTURED GOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has received a number of representations from auto dealers and others concerning recovery of tax which had
been paid on goods in their inventories on budget night. The matter has received careful consideration.
It is customary for changes in sales and excise taxes on commodities to come into effect on the day following the budget announcement. The government was aware that there would be goods in the hands of wholesalers and retailers on budget night on which the tax had been paid at the 12 per cent rate. However, the government did not propose a refund of the difference between the tax previously paid at the old rate and the new rate. This would be difficult to do in a fair way because of the wide range of products and the large number of retailers and distributors involved.
Questions have been raised by hon. members and by some auto dealers concerning refunds which were paid to auto dealers in 1958 and 1961, and to retailers of heavy trucks in 1974, when taxes were reduced on these vehicles. The measures introduced in those years were specifically oriented toward the automotive and transportation equipment industries. The decisions to pay refunds in respect of tax paid inventories were taken in the context of the exceptional circumstances which had focused the tax cuts on the motor vehicle industry.
The situation today is not the same. The recent reduction in federal sales taxes affects a broad range of taxable goods. It was not specifically directed toward any one industry.
Hon. members will appreciate that it would be difficult to provide relief for tax-paid inventory for the auto industry without providing similar relief for all goods held in inventories in Canada. A general provision to provide refunds to wholesalers and retailers holding tax-paid inventories at the time of the budget would result in a substantial revenue loss. Furthermore, it would be difficult to do so in an equitable manner because of the large number of products and traders involved.
The budget bills will be before the House shortly. The hon. member will then be able to bring forward an amendment which would take into account the difficulties I have outlined tonight.
